attrs.ground_contact: research lineage covering utility interconnection, water, fibre, land, regulatory for a closed-land DC campus

nodes.label: Power availability is a dated conditional queue position, not a site attribute

attrs.missing_or_defect: Diligence memos record available MW as a property of the site. It is a revocable, dated, conditional grant from an oversubscribed third party, carrying a ramp schedule, curtailment terms, re-study triggers and cancellation clocks.
attrs.remedy: Record power as the 7-tuple (requested MW, studied MW, approved-to-energise MW, energisation date, ramp schedule, curtailment obligations, re-study/cancellation clocks). Never as a scalar.
attrs.ground_contact: ERCOT: 'As of November 18, 2025, ERCOT had identified 5,302 MW of large loads in this category, which constitutes approximately 2% of the total load in ERCOT's large load interconnection process.'

nodes.label: ERCOT energised large load = 5,302 MW ≈ 2% of large-load process total

attrs.ground_contact: verbatim: 'As of November 18, 2025, ERCOT had identified 5,302 MW of large loads in this category, which constitutes approximately 2% of the total load in ERCOT's large load interconnection process.'

nodes.label: ERCOT assessing >233 GW large-load interconnection requests, >70% data centres
nodes.source_location: reporting statement by ERCOT VP System Planning & Weatherization at 2025-12-09 board meeting; article published 2026-01-06

attrs.ground_contact: 'more than 233 GW of large load interconnection requests', 'more than 70% coming from data centers', nearly 300% increase over year-end 2024; ERCOT VP quoted 'We have outgrown the process that was established for reviewing these large loads.' and 'We don't expect all of those will materialize'

nodes.label: ERCOT projected large load by status: 33.6 GW (2026) rising to 225.8 GW (2030)
nodes.source_location: Rev. 12.15.25, p.5 chart 'Actual and Projected Large Load Growth 2022-2030', published 2025-11-18

nodes.label: Large-load interconnection is a distinct process from generator interconnection

attrs.missing_or_defect: Curricula and practitioners reason about a data-centre LOAD using published GENERATOR queue statistics (LBNL Queued Up, FERC Order 2023), because generator data is abundant and public while large-load queues are recent, patchy and often confidential. The processes have different jurisdiction (FERC vs state/utility), different studies, and different cancellation mechanics.
attrs.remedy: Teach the two processes side by side. Teach that co-location or net metering puts the project in BOTH simultaneously, with two counterparties and two independent cancellation clocks.
attrs.ground_contact: ERCOT: 'A new large load that would participate in a net metering arrangement with a new Generation Resource or Energy Storage Resource must be evaluated through the Large Load Interconnection Process, while the associated Generation Resource or Energy Storage Resource must go through the Generator Interconnection or Modification Process.'

nodes.label: No vendor-neutral, region-general treatment of large-load interconnection exists
nodes.source_location: Rev. 12.15.25 (the only detailed current public plain-language description found)

attrs.missing_or_defect: ERCOT is effectively the only US region publishing a detailed, current, plain-language large-load interconnection process description. Other regions have analogous gates that are undocumented publicly, so practitioners cannot learn the general shape.
attrs.remedy: Build a region-general model of the large-load gate stack (threshold -> studies -> review clock -> agreements -> energisation conditions -> ramp plan -> cancellation clocks) using ERCOT as the worked example, and teach students to go find each gate's local analogue.
attrs.ground_contact: Absence observed across searched sources; ERCOT doc is the outlier in specificity

nodes.label: FERC Order 2023 — generator interconnection cluster study reform

attrs.ground_contact: LBNL slide reproduces pro-forma stage durations: Cluster Request Window 45 days; Customer Engagement Window 60 days; Cluster System Impact Study 150 days; Affected System Study 150 days; Cluster Re-Study 150 days; Facility Study 90/180 days; Construction variable. Reforms listed: cluster studies, first-ready first-served, higher deposits & readiness criteria, financial penalties for transmission provider delay, heatmaps of available transmission capacity, improved affected system studies, GETs consideration. Compliance deadline May 2024. NOTE: I read LBNL's depiction, NOT the FERC order text itself.

nodes.label: Generator queue completion rate is low and regionally uneven (8-30% of capacity)
nodes.source_location: slides 8-9; requests submitted 2000-2018, status as of end-2023

attrs.missing_or_defect: Queue depth is routinely read as pipeline. Most of it never gets built.
attrs.remedy: Use completion rates, not queue GW, when reasoning about when new supply arrives in a region.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim slide 9: 'ISO-NE and ERCOT are the only regions with >20% of capacity reaching commercial operation date (COD)'. Project-count [capacity-weighted]: ISO-NE 31% [30%], ERCOT 30% [24%], PJM 24% [15%], MISO 21% [15%], West non-ISO 19% [10%], SPP 17% [14%], NYISO 15% [9%], Southeast 13% [10%], CAISO 12% [8%]. By type (count): Gas 31%, Wind 20%, Solar 13%, Battery 11%.

nodes.label: Median generator interconnection request to COD approaching 5 years

attrs.ground_contact: verbatim slide title: 'The median duration from interconnection request (IR) to commercial operations date (COD) continues to rise, approaching 5 years for projects completed in 2022-2023'. Regional medians (IR->COD, 2018-2023) highest CAISO/NYISO, lowest ISO-NE.

nodes.label: Generator queue entry windows were closed or deferred in several regions

attrs.missing_or_defect: A power plan that depends on new generation entering the queue may depend on a window that is administratively closed, independent of project merit.
attrs.remedy: Verify the queue window calendar for the specific region before assuming new supply can be requested at all.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim: PJM 'No new requests accepted in 2024 as they process backlog and begin transition clusters'; 'In 2022, PJM paused review of new requests until 2026'; CAISO 'Delayed Cluster 16 request application window from April 2024 (new date TBD)'; SPP 'Filed a waiver to delay closing of 2024 queue request window until March 2025, and defer opening the 2025 request window until April 2026'; MISO delayed 2023 request window until 2024.

nodes.label: ERCOT Planning Guide Section 9 / PGRR115 — Large Load Interconnection Process

attrs.ground_contact: OPEN standard, read directly. Threshold verbatim: 'one or more facilities at a single site with an aggregate peak demand greater than or equal to 75 MW behind one or more common points of interconnection or service delivery points.' PGRR115 effective 2025-12-15; 'does not apply to loads under 75 MW'. Approved by Texas PUC May 2025. Texas SB6 (2025 session) directs further PUC rulemaking (PUC Project No. 58481).

nodes.label: Study approval does not grant approval to energise — a separate gate stack follows

attrs.missing_or_defect: Schedules treat 'studies approved' as the interconnection milestone. It is not. Energisation requires a further stack: executed agreements, notice to proceed and financial security, inclusion in the Network Operations Model, verified telemetry, quarterly stability assessment, SSO studies/mitigation/monitoring, ride-through evaluation, and a current Load Commissioning Plan.
attrs.remedy: Model energisation as a distinct milestone with its own checklist and float. Never bind a lease or revenue date to study approval.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim Q&A: 'Q: Does ERCOT's approval of the final studies guarantee the large load customer approval to energize? A: No, there are additional steps described below that must be completed before a large load customer is authorized to energize.'

nodes.label: The Load Commissioning Plan gates MW ramp on third-party transmission upgrades

attrs.missing_or_defect: Financial models treat the MW ramp as a commercial assumption. It is a regulated schedule: each increment is gated on a transmission upgrade the customer does not control being placed in service, with written regulator approval required before each step up.
attrs.remedy: Underwrite the ramp curve against the utility's construction programme and equipment lead times, not against the lease-up plan. Treat the LCP as the authoritative revenue schedule.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim: 'A Load Commissioning Plan specifies the load increments and timeline by which the interconnecting large load customer intends to reach peak Demand.' / 'If the studies show that transmission upgrades are necessary for the full requested load to reliably interconnect, the TSP and interconnecting large load customer update the Load Commissioning Plan based on the date those upgrades are expected to be energized.' / 'the applicable TSP must notify ERCOT when a transmission upgrade identified in a Load Commissioning Plan becomes operational and seek ERCOT's written approval before increasing the large load customer's demand.'

nodes.label: Interconnection carries 180-day cancellation and 365-day re-study clocks

attrs.missing_or_defect: Construction delay is modelled as cost and schedule slip only. Past defined thresholds it becomes an existential risk to the interconnection itself and re-opens completed studies.
attrs.remedy: Track the 180/365-day clocks as top-level project risks with named owners. Any construction slip must be assessed against them explicitly.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim: 'Planning Guide Section 9.4(9) requires that the interconnecting large load customer meet the relevant requirements in section 9.5 within 180 days. If the interconnecting large load customer has not met the requirements within 180 days, then ERCOT may notify the TSP that the project is subject to cancellation. If the TSP does not provide a project status update within 30 days, ERCOT may consider the project canceled.' and 'if the interconnecting large load customer has not met the requirements to energize in Planning Guide Section 9.6(1) within 365 days of the requested Initial Energization date used for the LLIS study, then the lead TSP must provide an opinion to ERCOT on whether any re-studies are needed.'

nodes.label: Re-study risk is exogenous — a neighbouring large load can re-open your studies

attrs.missing_or_defect: Schedule risk registers model only endogenous delay. The dominant re-study driver is a third party's commercial decision nearby, against which there is no contractual protection and no way to price except as contingency.
attrs.remedy: Carry explicit re-study schedule contingency sized to local large-load activity. Monitor neighbouring interconnection activity as a project risk feed.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim: 'A common reason re-studies are needed is that another large load customer in the same area becomes a "must-study" load while the interconnecting large load customer's studies are being conducted or under review. ... Due to the large size of these proposed loads (many requests are 1 GW or more), the inclusion or omission of even a single large load from another load's study can significantly change study outcomes. ... This situation is likely to occur in areas where several large load customers are seeking to interconnect.'

nodes.label: Accelerating the energisation schedule is itself a re-study trigger

attrs.missing_or_defect: Teams assume schedule compression is unilaterally available. Proposing to energise faster than studied is an enumerated material change requiring full or partial re-study — going faster can make you slower.
attrs.remedy: Route any proposed acceleration, load-type change, POI/SDP change, or control-system change through interconnection review before committing.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim material-change list: 'Changing the type of load (e.g., data center to hydrogen electrolyzer) or the mix of motor and power electronic load from what was studied.' / 'Changing the interconnection timeline significantly (especially if the customer is proposing to energize the load faster than what was studied).' / 'Proposing to change the Service Delivery Point or Point of Interconnection.' / 'Changing control systems that might materially impact the dynamic response of the site.'

nodes.label: Load Commissioning Plan / MW ramp gating is not taught

attrs.missing_or_defect: Curricula teach capacity planning as a static MW figure. The binding artefact is an incremental, regulator-approved ramp schedule tied to third-party upgrade in-service dates. Students are never shown one.
attrs.remedy: Teach the LCP as a first-class object: construct one from a study outcome, tie increments to upgrade dates, and show the revenue consequence of a slipped increment.
attrs.ground_contact: derived from directly-read ERCOT Planning Guide §9.2.4 description

nodes.label: Large electronic loads trip on voltage excursions; new ride-through rules are being imposed mid-build

attrs.missing_or_defect: A new class of technical obligation is being applied as a condition of energisation to projects already in construction, and failing it converts firm load into curtailable load rather than blocking energisation.
attrs.remedy: Make voltage/frequency ride-through capability an explicit diligence and procurement question before equipment selection, and track the governing revision request as a live project risk.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim: 'large electronic loads (LELs)—large consumers primarily using power electronics, such as data centers and cryptominers—have exhibited a tendency to trip during normal voltage excursions, presenting a risk to system stability.' / NOGRR282 'would apply to each large electronic load (LEL) as a condition for interconnection and continued operation', limited exemption for LELs approved to energise on or before 2025-11-14 / 'developers of LELs may need to modify their project designs or implement other measures to ensure they can comply with the final standards that are ultimately approved.' / 'If the model indicates the LEL will fail to ride through those simulated conditions, and that failure results in the violation of a System Operating Limit (SOL) or Interconnection Reliability Operating Limit (IROL), ERCOT will allow the load to energize subject to curtailment'

nodes.label: Ride-through failure converts firm load to curtailable load — a commercial outcome from an electrical property

attrs.missing_or_defect: The link from an equipment-level electrical characteristic selected years earlier to a permanent revenue-affecting service classification is not taught anywhere in site or facility curricula.
attrs.remedy: Teach the causal chain: power-electronics front-end behaviour -> dynamic model -> ride-through simulation -> SOL/IROL violation -> curtailable service classification -> revenue.
attrs.ground_contact: directly read ERCOT statement that failure results in energisation 'subject to curtailment'

nodes.label: Curtailability is a tradeable schedule asset — 76-215 GW of headroom exists at 0.25-5% curtailment
nodes.source_location: Norris, Duke Nicholas Institute, 'Rethinking Load Growth', presented 2025-03-27, slides 16-17

attrs.missing_or_defect: Curtailment is framed as a penalty to be bought out of. It is now the fastest available route to an earlier energisation date, and the quantitative case is public.
attrs.remedy: Evaluate curtailable service as a primary option at diligence, and identify which workloads are genuinely sheddable and who controls them.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim: '76 GW of headroom is available at an expected load curtailment rate of 0.25%. This headroom increases to 98 GW at 0.5% curtailment, 126 GW at 1.0%, and 215 GW at 5.0% curtailment.' / '88% of hours during which load curtailment is required retain at least half of the new load' / '60% of the hours retain at least 75% of the load, and 29% retain at least 90% of the load'

nodes.label: Curtailment hours/year: 85 h at 0.25%, 177 h at 0.5%, 366 h at 1.0%

attrs.ground_contact: chart values, avg across BAs: at 0.25% limit — 85 h any curtailment, 73 h with >=50% load remaining, 50 h >=75%, 24 h >=90%. At 0.5% — 177/155/106/52. At 1% — 366/323/224/110.

nodes.label: Curtailment-enabled headroom by balancing authority at 0.5% curtailment (GW)

attrs.ground_contact: PJM 17.8, MISO 14.8, ERCOT 10.0, SPP 9.7, SOCO 7.7, CAISO 5.0, TVA 4.5, FPL 4.2, NYISO 4.0, ISNE 3.5, DEC 2.8, DEF 2.1, BPA 1.9, AZPS 1.6, PACE 1.5, SRP 1.5, DEP 1.3, PSCO 1.2, PACW 1.0, PGE 0.9, SCP 0.7, DESC 0.6. Across 22 analysed balancing authorities.

nodes.label: US balancing authorities operate at 53% average load factor (range 43-61%)

attrs.ground_contact: verbatim: 'Aggregate load factors range between 43% to 61%, with an average and median value of 53%' and 'Winter load factors were notably lower than summer (59% vs. 63% average)'. This is the mechanism behind curtailment-enabled headroom.

nodes.label: Decision: accept curtailable/non-firm service to advance the energisation date
nodes.source_location: FERC order of 2025-12-18 directing PJM tariff revisions

attrs.remedy: Decide early, because it changes the study request itself. Requires the compute operator — not the real-estate entity — to underwrite the shed obligation.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim: new 'Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service' and 'Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service'; interim non-firm service as 'a bridge to more permanent transmission service'; non-firm customers 'will be curtailed during emergency operations before firm customers are curtailed'. Compliance filings due 2026-01-17 and 2026-02-16. NOTE: read a law-firm summary, not the FERC order text.

nodes.label: Curtailment commitments must be underwritten by whoever schedules the compute
nodes.source_location: slides 11-14 (flexibility types: on-site power/storage, temporal, spatial, reduced operations)

attrs.missing_or_defect: A shed obligation signed by a real-estate or colocation entity that does not control workload scheduling is unenforceable in practice and will be breached. The org-boundary problem is never taught.
attrs.remedy: Teach flexibility as a contractual chain: tariff obligation -> landlord -> tenant -> workload scheduler. Identify which of the four flexibility types (on-site power/storage, temporal, spatial, reduced operations) the actual tenant can deliver.
attrs.ground_contact: Duke taxonomy of flexibility types read directly; the org-boundary failure is inferred

nodes.label: Long-lead grid equipment, not construction, sets the MW ramp
nodes.source_location: slide 7 'Load growth is colliding with resource constraints' (citing NIAC 2024, Wood Mackenzie 2024, Li et al. 2024, Saul 2024, WECC 2024)

attrs.missing_or_defect: Site schedules are built around building construction. The binding constraint is utility-side equipment the developer does not order and cannot expedite.
attrs.remedy: Obtain the utility's equipment procurement status for every upgrade named in the Load Commissioning Plan before committing to a ramp curve.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim: 'Transformer order lead times have risen to 2-5 years—up from less than one year in 2020—while costs have surged by 80% (NIAC 2024)'; 'Lead times for high-voltage circuit breakers reached 151 weeks in late 2023, marking a 130% year-over-year increase (Wood Mackenzie 2024)'; 'Interconnection wait times have grown significantly, with some utilities reporting delays up to 7 to 10 years (Li et al. 2024; Saul 2024; WECC 2024)'

nodes.label: Network upgrade cost scales superlinearly with distance to strong transmission
nodes.source_location: slide 14, network cost mean $2022/kW vs distance to nearest 345 kV+ line, SPP and PJM

attrs.missing_or_defect: 'Distance to substation' is treated as a linear, minor cost factor. Observed generator data shows roughly 2-5x cost escalation from adjacent to >35 km, with PJM showing ~4.5x.
attrs.remedy: Use distance-to-strong-bus as an order-of-magnitude cost prior, and separately ask what is physically AVAILABLE at that substation (spare bay, spare transformer capacity, committed capacity, new-bay queue) — a close substation with no spare position is worse than a distant one with capacity.
attrs.ground_contact: slide 14 chart, mean $2022/kW by distance bucket. SPP: (0,1] ~150, (1,5] ~155, (5,15] ~160, (15,35] ~230, (35,inf) ~270. PJM: (0,1] ~150, (1,5] ~120-130, (5,15] ~225, (15,35] ~260, (35,inf) ~570. LBNL hypothesis verbatim: 'Renewables are often located in more rural areas where the existing transmission system is weaker, requiring costlier network upgrades.' CAVEAT: these are GENERATOR interconnection costs; load cost-causation differs.

nodes.label: Substation spare capacity and committed capacity, not distance, is the real diligence question
nodes.source_location: slide 14 (distance analysis) — the gap is what the analysis omits

attrs.missing_or_defect: Site-selection material teaches 'proximity to substation' as the metric. It omits spare bay positions, spare transformer capacity, capacity already committed to other customers, and the lead time for a new bay — all of which dominate distance.
attrs.remedy: Teach a substation interrogation checklist: available bay positions, transformer nameplate vs committed load, planned upgrades and their in-service dates, other pending large-load requests on the same bus.
attrs.ground_contact: inferred from the combination of the LBNL distance analysis and ERCOT's must-study/neighbour re-study mechanics

nodes.label: 40 CFR 63.6640(f) — emergency stationary RICE operating hour limits (NESHAP ZZZZ)

attrs.ground_contact: OPEN regulation, read directly. verbatim (f)(2): 'You may operate your emergency stationary RICE for the purpose specified in paragraph (f)(2)(i) of this section for a maximum of 100 hours per calendar year.' (f)(3): the 50 non-emergency hours 'are counted as part of the 100 hours per calendar year for maintenance and testing.' Restriction verbatim: 'The 50 hours per year for non-emergency situations cannot be used for peak shaving or non-emergency demand response, or to generate income for a facility to supply power to an electric grid or otherwise supply power as part of a financial arrangement with another entity.'

nodes.label: Emergency-generator hour limits block using gensets as grid flexibility

attrs.missing_or_defect: Flexibility and bridge-power strategies routinely assume the backup generator fleet can run to shave peaks or support the grid. Under emergency-engine status that is expressly prohibited, and exceeding the limits reclassifies the engines as non-emergency sources with far heavier permitting.
attrs.remedy: Decide the generator classification (emergency vs non-emergency/synthetic minor) at diligence, because it determines both the air-permit path and whether gensets can serve as curtailment response. The two strategies are mutually exclusive under emergency status.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim CFR: 'cannot be used for peak shaving or non-emergency demand response, or to generate income for a facility to supply power to an electric grid or otherwise supply power as part of a financial arrangement with another entity.' EPA page verbatim: 'Emergency engines may operate for 100 hr/yr for maintenance/testing' and '50 hr/yr of the 100 hr/yr allocation can be used for: non-emergency situations if no financial arrangement'.

nodes.label: Generator classification couples the air permit to the grid-flexibility strategy

attrs.missing_or_defect: Air permitting and grid strategy are taught as separate domains. In fact one binary choice — emergency vs non-emergency engine classification — simultaneously determines permit burden, allowed run hours, and whether the site can offer generator-backed curtailment response. Nobody teaches this coupling.
attrs.remedy: Teach generator classification as a single cross-domain decision node with both an environmental-permitting branch and a grid-services branch, made before equipment procurement.
attrs.ground_contact: inferred from directly-read CFR text plus the curtailment/flexibility material

nodes.label: Queue depth overstates real competition but not study burden

attrs.missing_or_defect: A developer shopping the same load to four utilities appears four times in four queues. Published queue GW is therefore inflated as a measure of competing demand — but the duplicate requests still consume study resources and still trigger must-study re-studies, so they delay you regardless.
attrs.remedy: Teach the distinction: discount queue depth when forecasting competition for capacity; do NOT discount it when forecasting study timelines.
attrs.ground_contact: ERCOT VP verbatim: 'We don't expect all of those will materialize, so it's very important to get those load forecasting and standardization rules in place.'

nodes.label: FERC Order 2023 available-transmission-capacity heatmaps
nodes.source_location: slide 16, 'Visual representation (heatmaps) of available transmission capacity'

attrs.remedy: Use published heatmaps as a pre-acquisition screen so that 'is there a strong bus here' is answered before land money is committed rather than after.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim reform bullet in LBNL summary of Order 2023

nodes.label: LBNL Queued Up public interconnection queue dataset
nodes.source_location: dataset landing page (page itself returned HTTP 403 to automated fetch; identified via the LBNL presentation's citation)

attrs.remedy: Use for regional supply-arrival forecasting and completion-rate priors. Does NOT cover large loads.
attrs.ground_contact: cited on LBNL presentation slide 18 as the source for queue analysis and data; underlying figures read from the presentation itself

nodes.label: ERCOT monthly Actual and Projected Large Load Growth chart

attrs.remedy: Track monthly to observe conversion between statuses; the ratio of 'Observed Energized' to total is the honest denominator for 'is power available here'.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim: 'ERCOT publishes a chart each month showing the growth in large load over time.' Five status categories: No Studies Submitted, Under ERCOT Review, Planning Studies Approved, Approved to Energize but Not Operational, Observed Energized.

nodes.label: Route diversity is a geographic fact; carrier count is a commercial fact

attrs.missing_or_defect: Diligence records carrier count as if it were failure-domain count. Named collapse modes: collapsed ring (both legs spliced in one sheath), last-hundred-metres convergence into one trench/bridge/rail easement, single lead-in vault forcing one wall penetration, shared sleeve through the building shell, and shared node (both circuits on one aggregation router or MMR).
attrs.remedy: Record N = proven-disjoint physical paths, never carrier count. Require physical trace, not attestation.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim: 'Carrier diversity is a contract. Route diversity is geography, and only a physical trace proves it.' / 'most metro and middle-mile capacity is leased, resold, and consolidated, so two competing names routinely deliver from the same trench.' / 'field audits regularly find both sides of the ring spliced inside a single cable sheath.' CAVEAT: sources are consultants and fibre operators with commercial interest in selling diversity; doctrine is uncontested but weakly evidenced in the terrestrial enterprise domain.

nodes.label: No published post-mortem exists of contractually diverse terrestrial circuits failing through a proven shared conduit
nodes.source_file: negative finding across the fibre research pass

attrs.missing_or_defect: The route-diversity doctrine is taught as established fact but rests on consultant assertion, anonymised anecdote, and submarine-cable analogues. No publicly published enterprise or data-centre incident report was found proving contractually diverse circuits failed together via a shared conduit.
attrs.remedy: Teach the doctrine with its evidentiary status stated, and use the well-documented submarine corridor events as the rigorous proof of principle. Commission or surface a terrestrial case study.
attrs.ground_contact: explicit negative finding after targeted search; the strongest terrestrial proxy found (Howard Street Tunnel 2001) names only ONE carrier in the source actually read

_provenance: negative finding across the fibre research pass

nodes.label: SRG-diverse routing is NP-complete — carriers cannot compute, and are not permitted to verify, cross-carrier diversity

attrs.missing_or_defect: Buyers ask carriers to certify the property being bought. Carriers cannot in general compute guaranteed diversity even over their own plant, and will not show plant to a competitor — so no carrier can verify non-overlap with another carrier.
attrs.remedy: Treat diversity verification as an OWNER-SIDE obligation. Only the customer, under NDA with both carriers, can perform the overlay. Budget for it as an owner scope item.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim: 'SRG diverse routing problem has proven to be NP-complete.' / protection path 'cannot go through the same SRLG or SRNG.' Three relevant sub-types: SRLG (shared conduit/pole), SRNG (shared node), SREG (shared equipment).

nodes.label: Red Sea anchor drag severs three independent cable systems (2024-02-24)

attrs.ground_contact: verbatim: damaged cables were 'the Seacom/Tata cable, the Asia Africa Europe-1 (AAE-1), and the Europe India Gateway (EIG)'; cause 'the cables were cut by the anchor of the Rubymar, a cargo ship that was damaged by a ballistic missile on February 18.' Operator telemetry source.

nodes.label: West Africa rock falls sever four independent cable systems (2024-03-14)

attrs.ground_contact: verbatim: 'the Africa Coast to Europe (ACE), Submarine Atlantic 3/West Africa Submarine Cable (SAT-3/WASC), West Africa Cable System (WACS), and MainOne cables were all damaged'; 'reportedly caused by underwater rock falls'; 'impacted 13 African countries'. Restoration: SAT-3 6 Apr, ACE 17 Apr, WACS and MainOne expected 28 Apr — roughly six weeks.

nodes.label: Nashville AT&T facility bombing — single address as a regional failure domain (2020-12-25)
nodes.source_location: reporting on Tennessee board findings; corroborated at https://www.pbs.org/newshour/amp/nation/widespread-outages-continue-in-tennessee-following-blast

attrs.remedy: Obtain the CISA communications-dependencies case study PDF (returned HTTP 403 to automated retrieval) before teaching this case in detail.
attrs.ground_contact: outages at 66 public-safety answering points; customers 'lost service — phones, internet or video — across large parts of Tennessee, Kentucky and Alabama'; FAA halted flights out of Nashville. Facility-level rather than conduit-level concentration risk.

nodes.label: Fibre diligence must precede site control — lateral permitting alone is 12-24 months

attrs.missing_or_defect: Unlike power, fibre has no public queue and no public dataset, so it is the constraint most absent from early underwriting and most likely to surface late. A campus can be acquired that cannot serve its intended tenant at any price.
attrs.remedy: Prove at least two physically disjoint lateral paths BEFORE site control, not after.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim: 'Permitting and engineering can take 12–24 months, especially in dense urban areas.' / 'underground FTDC fiber costs $60,000–$120,000 per mile on average.' / 'up to 45% of total capex goes toward civil engineering: trenching, boring, traffic control.' / 'Fiber is the constraint most consistently absent from early-stage underwriting and most likely to surface catastrophically late.' CAVEAT: trade analysis without primary citation — planning-grade, not bankable.

nodes.label: Railroad crossings have no federal shot clock and no fee cap — an unbounded schedule item
nodes.source_location: 2025-11-17, quoting Ray LaMura, president, Broadband Association of Virginia

attrs.missing_or_defect: Neither the FCC nor the FRA has authority over fibre crossings of railroad right-of-way, so there is no shot clock and no fee cap. Worse, NO defensible duration figure exists in the public sources — schedules that assign a number to a railroad crossing are assigning a number nobody has published.
attrs.remedy: Treat each railroad crossing as an unbounded serial negotiation with a named owner and no assumed duration. Do not model on the assumption the pending RAIL Act will pass.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim on-the-record quotes: 'The railroad quoted $600,000. That wiped out the entire grant budget.' / 'They charge excessive fees—hundreds of thousands of dollars—just to cross' / 'construction stopped on multiple projects while litigation dragged on' / 'One provider just gave up and walked away.'

nodes.label: Fibre permitting volume: median 8 authorities per build; 4,964 road and 3,072 railroad crossings across BEAD projects
nodes.source_location: reporting 2026-08-06 on Advanced Communications Law & Policy Institute (ACLP), New York Law School study of 6,933 terrestrial BEAD project areas against 126 permitting layers

attrs.remedy: Retrieve the ACLP primary report; these figures were read via trade summary.
attrs.ground_contact: over 86,000 permits across all BEAD projects; >half of projects need 10+ permits; 1 in 7 need 20+; median 8 separate authorities. Federal environmental review 95% of projects, state 76%, private/third-party agreements 71%, county 100%. Road/highway crossings 4,964 projects; railroad crossings 3,072. CAVEAT: BEAD is rural last-mile; per-authority and per-crossing structure transfers to a campus lateral, the build profile does not.

nodes.label: Route diversity and crossing schedule are in direct tension
nodes.source_location: synthesis of crossing-permit findings with route-diversity requirement

attrs.missing_or_defect: Crossings are treated as additive-independent schedule items. They are serial third-party negotiations, at least the railroad ones unbounded. A genuinely disjoint second route requires its OWN crossings at its own unbounded risk — so the diversity requirement makes the schedule worse, not better. Curricula teach diversity as a design requirement without pricing its schedule cost, which is how projects end up with one route and a diversity letter.
attrs.remedy: Teach diversity and crossing schedule as a single joint optimisation with an explicit trade-off, not as independent requirements.
attrs.ground_contact: inferred from directly-attributed crossing testimony plus the diversity requirement

nodes.label: Single-mode fibre propagation ≈ 4.9 µs/km one-way (≈9.8 µs/km round trip)

attrs.remedy: Use ROUTE km not great-circle km, and add fixed per-hop equipment delay (transponder DSP, FEC, amplification). The commonly used 1.3-1.6x route factor is an unverified rule of thumb.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim: 'using 4.9 microseconds per kilometer with 1.47 as the refractive index'; 'you can use 5 microseconds per kilometer as a rounded guide'; worked example '100km ... would result in a latency of 489.34µs'.

nodes.label: Latency sensitivity is far narrower than site selection assumes — $300M bought 1.5 ms
nodes.source_location: Chicago to Carteret NJ dark fibre build

attrs.missing_or_defect: Site selection routinely treats 'distance to a peering hub' as a hard constraint for workloads that have no latency budget. The only well-documented case where milliseconds justified capital is electronic trading.
attrs.remedy: Make latency a hard constraint only where a NAMED workload has a NAMED budget. Otherwise it is a tiebreaker.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim: '827 miles (1,331 km)' built for 'US$300 million', delivering '13 milliseconds' vs '14.5 milliseconds'. The entire premium was 1.5 ms — about 150 route-km at 9.8 µs/km RTT.

nodes.label: AI training vs inference latency sensitivity is unsourced
nodes.source_file: negative finding across the fibre research pass

attrs.missing_or_defect: No citable source was obtained on AI training latency tolerance vs inference latency sensitivity. The adjacent weak signal is that AI campuses are BANDWIDTH-constrained rather than latency-constrained, which would redirect diligence to fibre count and conduit capacity rather than kilometres to a hub — but that rests on a single weak claim.
attrs.remedy: Do not present this as answered. Source it properly before any curriculum asserts a latency requirement for AI workloads.
attrs.ground_contact: explicit retrieval failure (NVIDIA and Ciena sources 404/403); flagged rather than filled

_provenance: negative finding across the fibre research pass

nodes.label: PeeringDB reports Equinix Ashburn IX at 347 peers, 423 connections, 29.0 Tbps headline capacity

attrs.remedy: Prefer participant count and facility presence over capacity headline for site selection.
attrs.ground_contact: primary registry: '347 peers with 423 total connections; 184 are open peers'; 'Total Capacity 29.0T'; 82% IPv6. Fabric spans Equinix DC1-DC15, DC21-DC22 Ashburn, DC16, and CU1-CU4 Culpeper — already extended ~60 miles southwest.

nodes.label: APNIC ranks Equinix Ashburn 13th globally at 5.7 Tbps, behind Chicago at 6.4 Tbps
nodes.source_location: Gael Hernandez, 2026-06-26, ranking derived from PeeringDB data

attrs.ground_contact: verbatim framing: 'Sourced from PeeringDB, the table below ranks the networks with the largest deployed port capacity at IXPs.' Top: IX.br Sao Paulo 22.8 Tbps; DE-CIX Frankfurt 11.0; Equinix Singapore 10.9. Equinix Chicago rank 9 (6.4 Tbps); Equinix Ashburn rank 13 (5.7 Tbps); Equinix Dallas rank 14 (5.7 Tbps).

nodes.label: The 'distance to Ashburn' heuristic is justified by data that does not support it
nodes.source_location: ranking table vs common site-selection practice

attrs.missing_or_defect: Public-IX capacity data puts Chicago above Ashburn and Dallas level with it. Ashburn's genuine primacy is in private interconnection and cloud on-ramp density — which PeeringDB does not measure. The heuristic may be right, but the evidence usually cited for it is the wrong evidence.
attrs.remedy: Teach the metric limits: public IX capacity is not private interconnection density. Source the on-ramp argument separately or drop the claim.
attrs.ground_contact: derived from the two directly-read capacity sources; the private-interconnection explanation is INFERRED and labelled as such

nodes.label: ANSI/TIA-942-C — data centre telecommunications infrastructure standard (Rated-1..4)

attrs.missing_or_defect: PAYWALLED — standard text NOT read. No clause or section number is cited anywhere in this fragment or the accompanying prose, by design.
attrs.remedy: TIA-942 addresses entrance-facility and pathway redundancy tied to rating level per vendor summaries. Purchase the standard before asserting any specific requirement, separation distance, or count.
attrs.ground_contact: UNGROUNDED for requirements. Independently confirmed from the open TIA page only: TIA-942-C 'was published in May, 2024' and defines four Data Center Infrastructure Ratings (Rated-1 Basic, Rated-2 Redundant Component, Rated-3 Concurrently Maintainable, Rated-4 Fault Tolerant). Useful staleness detector: any TIA-942 requirement quoted in 'Tier 1-4' language is from a superseded revision.

nodes.label: Entrance room and meet-me room are conflated; a single MMR is a shared-risk node
nodes.source_location: definitional page; MMR schedule point from https://build.inc/insights/meet-me-room-data-center (2026-06-28)

attrs.missing_or_defect: Entrance room (OSP demarcation) and meet-me room (interconnection fabric) are distinct. A campus can have two properly separated entrance rooms and still funnel everything through one MMR — an SRNG that defeats the entrance diversity. Separately, entry geometry is a SHELL schedule item, not a fit-out item.
attrs.remedy: Model ER and MMR as separate nodes with separate redundancy requirements. Lock entry-point and MMR geometry before the building envelope is final.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim definitions: MMR is 'the designated space where multiple telecommunications providers... interconnect—often via cross-connects'; Entrance Room is 'the secure gateway for external telecom services entering the data center... first point of demarcation'. Schedule point verbatim: 'If two routes converge in the same duct bank or share the same sleeve through the shell, that is not diversity.' / 'Once the shell is closed, MMR options become expensive fast.' / 'Lock these items before the envelope is final.'

nodes.label: IRU repair and O&M cost pass-through is irrefusable — route exposure is a recurring liability

attrs.missing_or_defect: IRUs are underwritten as capacity assets. The holder must pay a share of maintenance and post-mishap repair costs, and those charges are irrefusable — so a physically exposed route (bridge-hung, shallow, high dig-density) is a recurring liability, not merely a risk.
attrs.remedy: Diligence the physical protection of the route before valuing the IRU, not only its capacity and term.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim: IRU is 'the exclusive, unrestricted, and indefeasible right to use the relevant capacity'; terms 'commonly lasting 20 to 30 years'; holder must 'pay a portion of the operating costs, and the costs of maintaining the cable, including any costs incurred repairing the cable after mishaps', which are 'payable and irrefusable'; IRUs appear in 'tangible assets on a firm's balance sheet' and 'can be resold, traded or used as collateral'.

nodes.label: SRLG/SRNG/SREG shared-risk modelling

attrs.remedy: Require an explicit SRLG statement as a diligence artefact, and treat its absence as an unverified diversity claim.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim provisioning rule: 'the protection path must provide 100% SRG protection' and 'cannot go through the same SRLG or SRNG.'

nodes.label: Owner-side KMZ/GIS route overlay plus physical trace

attrs.remedy: Five evidence layers, each graded confirmed/qualified/unverified/contradicted: commercial (orders, service IDs, contracts, demarcation records); facility entry (drawings, entry-point identifiers, operator attestation, witnessed observation); internal paths (cross-connect records, MMR assignments, pathway statement, inspection); external routing (route-diversity letter, carrier engineering attestation, controlled map review); full dependency (end-to-end design review, SRLG statement, upstream and cloud termination records, failover test).
attrs.ground_contact: artefact lists read verbatim. Key question verbatim: 'What exact meaning does each provider assign to "diverse," "protected" or "redundant"?' and 'What shared ducts, bridges, poles, aggregation sites or regeneration facilities are known?' KMZ alone is insufficient — it stops at each carrier's network boundary and lacks last-hundred-metres resolution.

nodes.label: EPA Seitz memorandum (1995) — Calculating Potential to Emit for Emergency Generators
nodes.source_location: Memorandum, John S. Seitz, Director OAQPS, 1995-09-06

attrs.ground_contact: OPEN document, read directly. verbatim: 'The EPA believes that 500 hours is an appropriate default assumption for estimating the number of hours that an emergency generator could be expected to operate under worst-case conditions... These calculations indicate that these generators, in and of themselves, rarely emit at major source levels. (Of course, there may be unusual circumstances where these calculations would not be representative, for example where many generators are present that could operate simultaneously).'

nodes.label: A genset fleet aggregates into one stationary source and can trigger PSD major-source review
nodes.source_location: 1995 Seitz memo final parenthetical; thresholds at 40 CFR 52.21(b)(1)(i) via https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/40/52.21

attrs.missing_or_defect: Generators are assessed individually, where each is trivially minor. Potential-to-emit aggregates across the fleet under the same-source test, and data centres are NOT a listed source category so the greenfield attainment-area threshold is 250 tpy. Nesting trap: adding on-site combined-cycle or steam-electric generation puts the campus in a LISTED category and drops the threshold to 100 tpy — so the bring-your-own-power strategy can silently make the air permit harder.
attrs.remedy: Compute fleet PTE at diligence, before genset count and site generation strategy are fixed. Establish whether synthetic-minor limits are achievable and federally enforceable.
attrs.ground_contact: EPA's own 1995 parenthetical anticipates the fact pattern: 'there may be unusual circumstances where these calculations would not be representative, for example where many generators are present that could operate simultaneously'. PTE definition requires limits to be 'federally enforceable' to count.

nodes.label: EPA 2019 adjacency guidance — physical proximity, no bright line, state discretion retained
nodes.source_location: Memorandum, Anne L. Idsal, Acting Assistant Administrator, to Regional Administrators 1-10, 2019-11-26

attrs.ground_contact: OPEN document, read directly. verbatim: 'EPA is not here establishing or recommending a "bright line," or specifying a fixed distance, within which two or more properties will be deemed (or presumed) by EPA to be in close enough physical proximity to be considered "adjacent."' and 'State, local, and tribal permitting authorities... are not required to apply the interpretation set forth in this memorandum and retain discretion...' Also abandons functional interrelatedness: 'for those properties not in physical proximity to each other, EPA will not invoke the existence of some functional interrelationship to establish "adjacency."'

nodes.label: Campus phasing geometry can change the air permit class, with no federal bright line

attrs.missing_or_defect: Whether a phased multi-building campus is one source or several is a state-discretionary judgement with no federal distance rule. Phasing plans are drawn for construction and capital convenience by people who do not know they are setting the permit class.
attrs.remedy: Draw phasing geometry with the air consultant present. Where the state publishes benchmarks, use them (Virginia: 0.25+ miles generally NOT adjacent; under 0.125 miles generally adjacent) and treat their absence elsewhere as an open risk.
attrs.ground_contact: EPA's explicit refusal to set a distance read directly; Virginia benchmarks are a law-firm paraphrase, NOT verbatim DEQ text — flagged as such.

nodes.label: EPA 2025 fact sheet — use of backup generators to maintain electric grid reliability
nodes.source_location: FACT SHEET AND FREQUENTLY ASKED QUESTIONS, 2025-05-01

attrs.ground_contact: OPEN document, read directly. Five CUMULATIVE conditions quoted verbatim: engine 'dispatched by the local balancing authority or local transmission and distribution system operator'; dispatch 'intended to mitigate local transmission and/or distribution limitations so as to avert potential voltage collapse or line overloads'; dispatch 'follows reliability, emergency operation, or similar protocols that follow specific North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC), regional, state, public utility commission or local standards or guidelines'; 'The power is provided only to the facility itself or to support the local transmission and distribution system'; owner 'identifies and records the entity that dispatches the engine'. Triggering example: Duke Energy PowerShare Mandatory 50. NARROW local-reliability carve-out, NOT general merchant demand response; the 50 hours still counts inside the 100.

nodes.label: The air permit enters the construction critical path precisely at generator pads and foundations
nodes.source_file: EPA letter, Aaron Szabo, Assistant Administrator, to Philip McNeely, Maricopa County Air Quality Department, 2025-09-02
nodes.source_location: 'begin actual construction' interpretation re TSMC; definition at 40 CFR 52.21(b)(11)

attrs.missing_or_defect: Teams treat the air permit as blocking all construction (over-conservative) or as blocking nothing (reckless). The actual boundary is precise: shell/core and grading are PARALLEL; generator pads, foundations, underground piping and generator installation are STRICTLY SERIAL behind the permit — and that node is late in construction, which is why it surprises people.
attrs.remedy: Sequence generator pads behind permit issuance explicitly in the CPM schedule. Do not rely on 'equity in the ground' for leverage — the doctrine expressly denies it.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim: the definition 'prohibits the initiation of physical on-site construction on an emissions unit and... this does not prohibit initiation of physical on-site construction of those parts of a facility that do not qualify as an emission unit'; permitting authority may allow 'the core and shell of a building, provided that... [it] does not involve the physical construction on an emission unit or the laying of underground piping or construction of supports and foundations that are part of any emissions unit'. Caveats verbatim: construction pre-permit is 'solely at TSMC's risk'; authority 'may not use... time and resources expended on construction prior to obtaining a permit (what EPA has called "equity in the ground") to justify... BACT or LAER determinations'; authority 'may require... modifying or rebuilding structures that TSMC has begun building prior to obtaining a permit'; and 'This communication of EPA's view is not a final agency action'.

_provenance: EPA letter, Aaron Szabo, Assistant Administrator, to Philip McNeely, Maricopa County Air Quality Department, 2025-09-02

nodes.label: The 'equity in the ground' doctrine denies sunk-cost leverage by design
nodes.source_file: EPA letter, Aaron Szabo to Maricopa County Air Quality Department, 2025-09-02

attrs.missing_or_defect: Developers assume building ahead of a permit creates negotiating leverage through sunk cost. EPA doctrine expressly forbids the permitting authority from crediting it, and permits demolition or rebuild. Building ahead buys schedule and exactly zero permit leverage — a counterintuitive result that is not taught.
attrs.remedy: Teach pre-permit construction as a pure schedule bet with no leverage upside and an explicit rebuild downside.
attrs.ground_contact: directly-read EPA letter language on 'equity in the ground'

_provenance: EPA letter, Aaron Szabo to Maricopa County Air Quality Department, 2025-09-02

nodes.label: Virginia tightens generator emissions ~10x while federal policy loosens
nodes.source_location: 2026-05-19 reporting on Virginia DEQ guidance and HB 507; Tier 2 baseline via https://trinityconsultants.com/resources/virginia-department-of-environmental-quality-releases-three-air-permitting-guidance-documents-for-data-centers/ (2025-02-11)

attrs.missing_or_defect: Virginia caps total generator hours at 500/yr including emergencies and has repudiated the low-run-hours premise entirely. HB 507 requires Tier 4-equivalent limits for applications on or after 2026-07-01, presumptive 0.60 g/hp-hr against a Tier 2 base of 6.0 g/bhp-hr NOx. This moves compliance from an operational limit (cheap) to SCR hardware (capital, footprint, urea logistics, redesign).
attrs.remedy: Never carry a national air-permit assumption into Virginia. Size SCR into the generator plant footprint and capital at diligence for any Virginia site.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim DEQ: 'DEQ has also considered the permit history and operating profile for data center gen-sets that now strongly indicate that gen-sets permitted as emergency units will be operated for extended periods under certain circumstances.' and 'DEQ anticipates that future data center permit applications will request that most of their backup gen-sets be permitted as non-emergency units under Virginia regulations.' As of 2025-11-24 Virginia DEQ listed 184 existing NSR permits and 21 active applications for data centres.

nodes.label: Federal air permitting policy loosened through 2025-2026
nodes.source_location: EPA news release 2025-09-09; proposed rule at https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-05-13/pdf/2026-09524.pdf; EO 14318 at https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/07/accelerating-federal-permitting-of-data-center-infrastructure/

attrs.missing_or_defect: Much of the loosening is PROPOSED or CONDITIONAL, not final. The 'Begin Actual Construction' redefinition was proposed 2026-05-13 and is not final; mobile-source reclassification is conditional on EPA later adopting nonroad standards for portable combustion turbines. Do not underwrite to either.
attrs.remedy: Track final-rule status before relying on any of it. Underwrite to current law.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim EPA 2025-09-09: 'This action provides flexibility to begin certain building activities that are not related to air emissions, such as installing cement pads, before obtaining a Clean Air Act (CAA) construction permit.' EO 14318 (2025-07-23) verbatim: 'Federal financial assistance representing less than 50 percent of total project costs shall be presumed not to constitute substantial Federal control and responsibility' — largely defederalising privately financed campuses.

nodes.label: By-right data-centre development is being withdrawn in major markets
nodes.source_location: Loudoun County CPAM-2024-0001 / ZOAM-2024-0001, adopted 2025-03-18 (7-2); analysis at https://www.mcguirewoods.com/client-resources/alerts/2025/4/loudoun-county-eliminates-by-right-use-for-data-centers-increasing-development-hurdles/

attrs.missing_or_defect: The largest data-centre market in the world moved the use from by-right to Special Exception in IP, GI and MR-HI districts. A discretionary approval is appealable, negotiable and politically reversible in a way a by-right permit is not. Grandfathering was narrow: applications before 2025-02-12, and only for sites more than 500 feet from residential.
attrs.remedy: Verify the entitlement pathway (by-right / conditional / rezoning) as a day-one diligence item, and price the discretionary-approval risk, not just the hearing calendar.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim: 'designate data centers as a conditional or Special Exception (SPEX) use in areas where the uses were previously allowed by-right'; 'special exceptions require a legislative process involving staff review and public hearings before the Planning Commission and the Board of Supervisors'. NOTE: Loudoun's substantive Phase 2 standards (generators, noise, screening, setbacks, height, cooling, lighting) were targeted for adoption December 2026 — any Loudoun dBA or setback figure circulating before then is NOT adopted code.

nodes.label: dBA code compliance and noise nuisance liability are different problems
nodes.source_location: equipment noise characterisation; litigation via https://www.classaction.org/data-center-noise-water-pollution-lawsuit and https://earthjustice.org/press/2024/granbury-residents-sue-local-bitcoin-mine-over-health-threatening-noise-pollution

attrs.missing_or_defect: Chillers and dry coolers run continuously and emit tonal, low-frequency content (reported 100-500 Hz band, plus 60 Hz transformer hum) that A-weighting systematically under-penalises relative to perceived annoyance. A facility can be simultaneously compliant on measured dBA and a sustained actionable nuisance. There is also NO national dBA number: enacted night limits found range 45 to 57+ dBA.
attrs.remedy: Design to perceived annoyance and tonal content, not only to the dBA limit. Model low-frequency and tonal components explicitly, and treat generator load-bank testing (reported 90-105 dBA at 25 ft for a 2 MW unit) as a separate scenario.
attrs.ground_contact: equipment figures from an advocacy aggregation (underlying sources not cited on the page) — MEDIUM confidence. Litigation is well attested: four data-centre noise nuisance class actions filed April-June 2026 (Haley v. X.AI Corp. N.D. Miss. ~2026-06-08; Demers v. Digi Power X, North Tonawanda NY, April 2026; Valenzuela v. Alliance Cloud Services, Dowagiac MI, May 2026; Montgomery v. DataOne USA, Vineland NJ, May 2026), with Citizens Concerned About Wolf Hollow v. Marathon Digital Holdings (Hood County TX, filed 2024-10-07) as the controlling continuous-fan-noise precedent.

nodes.label: Tonal noise penalty magnitude is contested (3 vs 5 vs 6 dB, different ISO bases)
nodes.source_file: PennFuture Model Data Center Ordinance (PDF returned unparseable) and Warrenton VA negotiated project condition via princewilliamtimes.com

attrs.missing_or_defect: None verified against primary ordinance text. Position A: flat 5 dB penalty under ISO 1996-2, triggered by any prominent tone via one-third octave analysis. Position B: 6 dB under ISO/TS 20065:2022, triggered only when narrow-band audibility reaches >=10 dB. Position C: 3 dB, negotiated as a project condition at Warrenton VA.
attrs.remedy: Verify against the governing local ordinance for the specific site before designing to any tonal penalty. Do not adopt a default.
attrs.ground_contact: UNGROUNDED on all three — candidate facts requiring primary verification

_provenance: PennFuture Model Data Center Ordinance (PDF returned unparseable) and Warrenton VA negotiated project condition via princewilliamtimes.com

nodes.label: Community procedural litigation costs two to three years, rarely the project
nodes.source_location: PW Digital Gateway litigation timeline; Warrenton delay via Citizens for Fauquier County reporting; aggregate via https://www.datacenterwatch.org/report and https://www.datacenterwatch.org/q3-q4-2025

attrs.missing_or_defect: Opposition is modelled as a binary approve/reject risk. The realistic outcome is delay: litigation attacks PROCEDURE (notice violations, legality of the zoning amendment, open-meetings acts), not merits, and reliably costs 2-3 years. Warrenton construction stalled ~3 years; Prince William County's own legal spend was reported over $1.72M across nearly 30 months.
attrs.remedy: Model opposition as a schedule distribution with a 2-3 year tail, not as a yes/no gate. Harden the procedural record (notice, hearings, minutes) as the primary defence.
attrs.ground_contact: DataCenterWatch aggregate: $18bn blocked and $46bn delayed May 2024-March 2025; at least $156bn blocked or delayed July-December 2025 with groups active in 42 states. NOTE: rolling report vintages with DIFFERENT windows — do not sum.

nodes.label: A local denial can be overridden by litigation or routed around at state level
nodes.source_file: Saline Township MI consent order (Judge Julia B. Owdziej, October 2025); Tucson Project Blue vote 2025-08-06 and subsequent Tucson Electric Power state-regulator route

attrs.missing_or_defect: Opposition case studies select on wins. Two counterexamples invert the lesson: Saline Township MI denied 4-1 (~Sept 2025) and the denial was REVERSED by litigation settlement/consent order (Oct 2025) — exclusionary-zoning litigation is a viable developer override. Tucson rejected Project Blue 7-0 (2025-08-06) but a related arrangement was pursued through STATE regulators — a municipal denial is not necessarily the end of development at the site.
attrs.remedy: Teach both directions. 'The council said no' and 'the project is dead' are different propositions, and the override paths are real and named.
attrs.ground_contact: Saline Township MED confidence (consent order reported, docket not verified); Tucson vote HIGH confidence with mayor on record: 'It is my responsibility to create guardrails to protect Tucson from this industry.' Also note Bessemer AL approved a $14bn campus 5-2 on 2025-11-18 DESPITE organised opposition.

_provenance: Saline Township MI consent order (Judge Julia B. Owdziej, October 2025); Tucson Project Blue vote 2025-08-06 and subsequent Tucson Electric Power state-regulator route

nodes.label: Data-centre moratoria and bans wave (2025-2026)
nodes.source_location: Hillsboro OR 2026-07-27; Prince George's County MD 2026-07-07; Holyoke MA 2026-06-17

attrs.remedy: Re-verify every entry before use — moratoria expire, extend, and multiply on a monthly cadence.
attrs.ground_contact: Prince George's County MD: two-year moratorium adopted 2026-07-07, extending a prior pause (HIGH). Holyoke MA: permanent ban on facilities >12 MW, 9-4, 2026-06-17 (HIGH). Hillsboro OR: 120 days with one 120-day extension possible, unanimous 2026-07-27, pending applications unaffected (HIGH). New York State: ~1 year, state environmental permits, >=50 MW (LOW-MED). nodes.label: Minimum-take tariffs convert the question from 'can we get power' to 'what is the take-or-pay exposure'
nodes.source_location: PUCO adoption of AEP Ohio Data Center Tariff 2025-07-09, effective 2025-07-23; Dominion GS-5 and Georgia PSC Rule 38

attrs.missing_or_defect: Dedicated large-load rate classes with minimum-take obligations are now standard and are set at state PUC level on roughly an annual cadence. AEP Ohio: minimum payment of 85% of subscribed monthly capacity for up to 12 years, loads over 25 MW. Dominion Virginia: new GS-5 class for 25 MW+, effective 2027-01-01. Georgia PSC Rule 38: above 100 MW, data centres pay T&D costs as construction progresses.
attrs.remedy: Underwrite take-or-pay exposure alongside the interconnection schedule, and stress-test it against a slipped Load Commissioning Plan increment.
attrs.ground_contact: AEP Ohio terms and PUCO adoption date HIGH confidence. SCC attorney on record re Dominion: 'Regardless of the cost allocation methodology that is chosen, there remains a glaring cross-class subsidization occurring to the benefit of new GS-5 customers.' Georgia Rule 38 aim: 'protect Non-Large Load customers from bearing any of the costs of adding the new Large Load customers.'

nodes.label: Minimum-take obligation can outrun the regulated MW ramp
nodes.source_location: synthesis of AEP Ohio 85%/12-year minimum with ERCOT Load Commissioning Plan mechanics

attrs.missing_or_defect: An 85%-of-subscribed-capacity minimum for 12 years, combined with a Load Commissioning Plan whose increments are gated on utility-controlled transmission upgrades, means the customer can be contractually obliged to pay for capacity the utility has not yet enabled it to draw. This interaction between tariff design and interconnection ramp is taught nowhere.
attrs.remedy: Negotiate minimum-take commencement against LCP increment milestones, not calendar dates. Teach the interaction explicitly as a worked example.
attrs.ground_contact: INFERRED by joining two directly-read sources (AEP Ohio tariff terms; ERCOT Planning Guide §9.2.4 ramp gating). No source found that names this interaction.

nodes.label: Sackett can remove the 404 nexus and with it the NEPA nexus entirely
nodes.source_location: 42 U.S.C. § 4336e(10)(A) federal nexus definition; Sackett v. EPA decided 2023-05-25 (tertiary source, primary opinion not fetched)

attrs.missing_or_defect: For a privately financed campus the usual federal nexus is an Army Corps 404 permit. Sackett narrowed WOTUS to relatively permanent, standing or continuously flowing waters — so for arid-region and upland sites the wetlands determination can remove the 404 nexus and therefore the NEPA nexus. That single determination is often the difference between a six-week and a two-year federal track.
attrs.remedy: Run the wetlands delineation as one of the earliest studies. It is the highest-leverage early determination in the regulatory domain.
attrs.ground_contact: nexus definition verbatim from statute: 'an action that the agency carrying out such action determines is subject to substantial Federal control and responsibility.' Sackett holding is from a tertiary source — MEDIUM confidence, primary opinion not read.

nodes.label: Section 404 permit duration is contested (Corps averages vs practitioner estimates)
