nodes.label: 42 U.S.C. § 4336a — NEPA statutory deadlines and page limits (Fiscal Responsibility Act 2023)

attrs.ground_contact: OPEN statute, read. verbatim: EIS 'not later than the date that is 2 years after the sooner of'; EA 'not later than the date that is 1 year after'; courts may 'set a schedule and deadline for the agency to act as soon as practicable, which shall not exceed 90 days'; 'an environmental impact statement shall not exceed 150 pages, not including any citations or appendices'; 300 pages 'of extraordinary complexity'; 'An environmental assessment shall not exceed 75 pages'.

nodes.label: CEQ NEPA regulations were rescinded — agency procedures now diverge

attrs.missing_or_defect: The familiar 75/150/300-page and 1/2-year figures originated in CEQ's 2020 regulations. CEQ rescinded its NEPA implementing regulations effective 2025-04-11. The numbers survive in statute; the CEQ regulatory authority does not. Any source describing them as 'CEQ regulatory limits' is citing repealed authority. Practical effect: agencies now run their own procedures, so a campus touching Corps 404 + DOE + FAA can face three inconsistent procedural regimes.
attrs.remedy: Cite 42 U.S.C. § 4336a, never the rescinded CEQ regulations. Map the specific procedures of each agency with a nexus to the project.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim: 'This interim final rule removes the Council on Environmental Quality (CEQ) regulations implementing the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) from the Code of Federal Regulations.' / 'This interim rule is effective April 11, 2025.' / 'CEQ has concluded that it may lack authority to issue binding rules on agencies in the absence of the now-rescinded E.O. 11991.'

nodes.label: Citizen-petition thresholds can force state environmental review cheaply

attrs.missing_or_defect: State environmental review is treated as a function of project characteristics. In Minnesota it can be triggered by a hundred signatures — a cheap, fast, statutorily hooked opposition lever that has no federal analogue and is not taught. Equivalent mechanisms in other states were not researched.
attrs.remedy: Inventory the citizen-trigger mechanisms in the specific state at diligence. Also note that California's AB 130 (2025) CEQA reform is HOUSING-ONLY and contains no data-centre exemption.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim: 'whenever material evidence accompanying a petition by not less than 100 individuals who reside or own property in a Minnesota county...demonstrates that...there may be potential for significant environmental effects'. Also: EIS 'must be prepared and its adequacy determined within 280 days after notice of its preparation unless the time is extended'. SEQRA (NY), MEPA (MA), SEPA (WA) NOT researched — explicit gap.

nodes.label: 40 CFR 312 — All Appropriate Inquiries / Phase I ESA validity windows

attrs.ground_contact: OPEN rule. Phase I must be 'conducted or updated within one year before the date of acquisition'; interviews, records review, inspection and lien search must be within '180 days before acquiring ownership'. CRITICAL POST-CLOSING NOTE: on a closed site the AAI clock has already run — a stale Phase I cannot be retroactively cured, and the bona fide prospective purchaser defence depends on having done it correctly BEFORE acquisition.

nodes.label: PJM interconnection timeline benchmark (RMI Speed to Power analysis)

attrs.remedy: Use as the regional schedule prior for PJM siting decisions.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim: 'the timeline from interconnection application to commercial operation has risen from an average of less than two years in 2008 to over eight years in 2025'. Cross-check from Data Center Knowledge 2026-05-12: 'AI infrastructure projects entering service in 2025 took an average of more than seven years to reach operational status, according to PJM Interconnection data'. NOT a contradiction — different populations (all requests vs AI projects reaching COD).

nodes.label: Transformer 128-week and GSU 144-week lead times; switchgear and genset backlogs (2025)
nodes.source_file: Wood Mackenzie Q2 2025 survey, cross-confirmed across two trade outlets

attrs.remedy: Order-position diligence, not catalogue lead time, is the schedule input.
attrs.ground_contact: 'Standard power transformers averaged 128-week lead times and GSUs averaged 144 weeks in Wood Mackenzie's Q2 2025 survey'. Switchgear: custom MV '70 to 100+ weeks'; mainstream MV '26-32 weeks (down from pre-COVID baseline of 12-16 weeks)'; Eaton data-centre backlog '228 GW — roughly twelve years of build at current rates'. Gensets: 'lead times for large units now sit in a 40 to 107-week band'; Cummins large genset allocation reportedly into 2028. REJECTED as a candidate fact: a '60 months' (~260 week) transformer figure ~80% above the corroborated range, could not be verified.

_provenance: Wood Mackenzie Q2 2025 survey, cross-confirmed across two trade outlets

nodes.label: Cooling architecture is the dominant water lever — ~140x spread on identical IT load
nodes.source_location: LBNL, 2024 United States Data Center Energy Usage Report, Figures 4.4 and 4.5, pp.39-48

attrs.missing_or_defect: Water demand is treated as a site property. It is a design choice. Median site WUE ranges from ~2.9-3.2 L/kWh (water-cooled chiller, no economizer) to ~0 (air-cooled chiller) — for a 100 MW IT load that is 2.54 billion L/yr versus ~17.5 million L/yr.
attrs.remedy: Treat cooling architecture as the primary water decision and evaluate it jointly with the PUE/MW consequence in the interconnection analysis.
attrs.ground_contact: OPEN report, read directly (PDF text extraction plus figure rendering). Definition verbatim: 'Water Usage Effectiveness is similarly defined as the total water consumption of the data center divided by the electricity demand of the IT equipment... WUE is reported in terms of liters per kWh.' NOTE the denominator is IT electricity, not total facility. Printed Figure 4.5 values for 2023: Small PUE 1.91 / WUE 0.32; Midsize+Colo 1.68 / 0.67; Hyperscale 1.22 / 0.32; AI Specialized 1.14 / 0.61. Figure 4.4 medians are CHART READS, approximate to ~+/-0.1.

nodes.label: Liquid cooling does not reduce water if heat is rejected evaporatively

attrs.missing_or_defect: Industry framing presents liquid cooling as a water-saving technology. LBNL's data shows AI Specialized has the LOWEST PUE of any class (1.14) and nearly the HIGHEST WUE (0.61) — roughly double hyperscale's 0.32. The fleet-average WUE is forecast to RISE from ~0.36 to 0.45-0.48 L/kWh, attributed specifically to liquid-cooled systems.
attrs.remedy: Teach that 'liquid cooling' describes heat capture at the chip, not heat rejection at the plant. Only IT liquid cooling with a dry cooler and air-cooled chiller is genuinely low-water (~0 WUE at PUE ~1.09).
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim: 'IT liquid cooling: waterside economizer (water-cooled chiller)... While highly energy-efficient, this system consumes substantial amounts of water, like all evaporative cooling systems.' and 'the average WUE rises slightly, reaching between 0.45 and 0.48 L/kWh, reflecting increasing WUEs in the hyperscale and colocation data centers, along with the increased water consumption of liquid-cooled systems.'

nodes.label: The water-for-energy trade can flip sign depending on grid water intensity

attrs.missing_or_defect: Going air-cooled to save site water costs energy, and that energy costs water elsewhere. Only about 61% of the apparent site-water saving survives at the US average indirect intensity, and above a break-even grid intensity of roughly 11.6 L/kWh going air-cooled consumes MORE total water than it saves.
attrs.remedy: Evaluate waterless cooling against the water intensity of the specific balancing authority being interconnected to, not against a national average. This ties the water decision directly back to the interconnection decision.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim: 'While air-cooled chillers use no water, they use more energy.' and 'In 2023, energy consumption by a data center translates to national average of 4.52 L/kWh of indirect water consumption'. Break-even and 61% figures are DERIVED ARITHMETIC on LBNL inputs (midsize WCC PUE ~1.57/WUE ~2.9 vs ACC PUE ~1.82/WUE ~0), labelled as such. LBNL caveat verbatim: the method 'does not incorporate any power purchase agreements between individual data center facilities and their electricity providers or on-site "behind the meter" generation, which could significantly affect water consumption and emissions estimates'. Corroborating spread from Siddik et al. 2021 (Environ. Res. Lett. 16 064017): 1 MWh requires 7.1 m3 water nationally, 'range 1.8-105.9 m3'.

nodes.label: The modelled WUE floor should not be underwritten — LBNL says so itself

attrs.missing_or_defect: The modelled ~0.02 L/kWh for airside economizer plus adiabatic is optimistic; operators report 0.1-0.3 L/kWh for similar systems. Curricula and pro formas quote the modelled floor.
attrs.remedy: Plan airside-economizer-plus-adiabatic at 0.1-0.3 L/kWh, not 0.02.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim: 'simulated PUEs assume systems are commissioned and operate as designed. This is rarely the case... Therefore, the actual PUEs (and WUEs) will likely not be as good as estimated' and 'Some hyperscale facilities report WUE values for similar systems of 0.1-0.3 L/kWh, which is much higher than the values simulated here'.

nodes.label: Water right seniority is a valid-as-of fact, not a constant — Idaho moved the cut-off 54 years in two years
nodes.source_location: IDWR Docket CM-DC-2010-001 final orders of 2024-05-30 and 2026-05-14 (https://idwr.idaho.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/CM-DC-2010-001-20260514-Final-Order-Curtailing-Ground-Water-Rights-Junior-to-October-11-1900.pdf)

attrs.missing_or_defect: A priority date is recorded as a permanent attribute of the right. It is only meaningful relative to a given year's call. A 1960 right was curtailed in 2024; a 1910 right was safe in 2024 and curtailed in 2026. Industrial AND municipal uses are expressly in scope, so taking city water is not a safe harbour.
attrs.remedy: Store priority-date adequacy with a valid_from/valid_to, never as a constant. Model curtailment exposure as a distribution over future calls.
attrs.ground_contact: OPEN orders, read directly. 2024 verbatim: 'ground water users holding water rights bearing priority dates junior to March 31, 1954... shall immediately curtail/refrain from diversion' and 'this order shall apply to consumptive ground water rights, including but not limited to, agricultural, commercial, industrial, and municipal uses.' 2026 verbatim: 'priority dates junior to October 11, 1900... shall curtail'. Enforcement is physical — status summaries distinguish wells the watermaster has and has not 'physically locked'.

nodes.label: Mitigation-plan membership beat priority date in practice

attrs.missing_or_defect: Prior appropriation is taught as strict priority ordering. In the 2024 Idaho call, allocation turned on collective mitigation-plan compliance: a hydrologically identical neighbour inside a complying district kept pumping. Rights models carry priority_date and omit mitigation_plan_membership.
attrs.remedy: Add mitigation_plan_membership as a first-class attribute of a water right. Teach the doctrine-versus-practice gap explicitly.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim: 'the Southwest Irrigation District, Coalition of Cities, Water Mitigation Coalition, and the American Falls-Aberdeen, Henrys Fork and Madison ground water districts continue to comply with approved mitigation plans and consequently are protected from curtailment.' and 'the groundwater districts facing curtailment ultimately chose not to comply with either of their plans in the manner required. As a result, many junior groundwater users will be curtailed who might otherwise have been spared.'

nodes.label: Curtailment law differs materially by state — 'prior appropriation' is not a sufficient classification
nodes.source_location: C.R.S. § 37-92-502(2)(a); contrast with Idaho computed-shortfall administration; RCW 90.03.010 for the hybrid case

attrs.missing_or_defect: Colorado requires material injury PLUS a futility check — a discontinuance 'shall be rescinded' if it does not actually deliver water to the senior. Idaho curtails on a computed methodology-order shortfall. Washington is HYBRID, preserving pre-existing riparian rights while establishing appropriation priority, and adds relinquishment ('use it or lose it') risk relevant to a phased campus.
attrs.remedy: Never generalise across prior-appropriation states. An identically-dated junior right carries materially different exposure in CO than ID.
attrs.ground_contact: Colorado verbatim: 'no such discontinuance shall be ordered unless the diversion is causing or will cause material injury' and 'if... such discontinuance does not cause water to become available to such senior priorities at the time and place of their need, then such discontinuance order shall be rescinded.' Washington verbatim (RCW 90.03.010): 'as between appropriations, the first in time shall be the first in right. Nothing contained in this chapter shall be construed to lessen, enlarge, or modify the existing rights of any riparian owner'.

nodes.label: Oregon inverted the burden of proof — absence of groundwater data is a denial, not neutrality
nodes.source_location: OWRD backgrounder on updated groundwater allocation rules, effective 2024-09-17

attrs.missing_or_defect: Site selection assumes an unstudied basin is an unconstrained one. In Oregon since 2024-09-17 the opposite holds: a greenfield site in a poorly monitored basin is WORSE positioned than one with data showing moderate decline.
attrs.remedy: Check basin monitoring coverage as a first-order screen in Oregon-type regimes, not just modelled availability.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim: 'If the Department is not able to make site-specific determinations based on existing data, a finding will be made that no water is available for the requested use and the application will be denied. In practice, this means overall fewer new water right applications will be granted.' CAVEAT: this quotes OWRD's plain-language backgrounder describing the rule, NOT the enacted rule text — the OAR text retrieved appeared to be a pre-2024 version.

nodes.label: Texas groundwater ownership does not convey a right to any specific yield

attrs.missing_or_defect: Landowner ownership is recognised as real property, then expressly decoupled from any capture entitlement. Districts permit up to a Desired Future Condition, and § 36.113(e) allows MORE restrictive conditions on NEW applicants — the newcomer is structurally disadvantaged. DFCs re-adopt on a five-year statutory cycle, so the modelled available groundwater underwritten against can be revised.
attrs.remedy: Underwrite Texas groundwater against the district's DFC/MAG cycle and its treatment of new applicants, not against acreage owned.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim § 36.002(b-1): the rights 'do not: (1) entitle a landowner... to the right to capture a specific amount of groundwater below the surface of that landowner's land'. § 36.113(e): a district 'may impose more restrictive permit conditions on new permit applications... to increase use by historic users'. § 36.108(d) sets the five-year DFC cycle. NOTE: statutes.capitol.texas.gov is an SPA serving no text to fetchers; texas.public.law reproduces the sections with official citations.

nodes.label: The Arizona AMA groundwater halt is a two-hop dependency, not a direct data-centre gate
nodes.source_location: ADWR Phoenix AMA groundwater supply updates (read via Internet Archive capture 2026-07-27, cross-checked against a 2024-12-28 capture); A.R.S. § 45-576 at https://www.azleg.gov/ars/45/00576.htm

attrs.missing_or_defect: The 2023 Phoenix AMA finding is widely misreported as a direct data-centre constraint. The Assured Water Supply certificate requirement attaches to SUBDIVIDERS; a data centre is not a subdivision. But the halt binds new AWS DESIGNATIONS, which municipal providers hold — so a data centre on municipal service is exposed indirectly through its provider's designated supply headroom.
attrs.remedy: Model as provider-headroom dependency, not as a direct permit gate. Note ADWR's 2024 update records industrial-sector unmet demand going UP.
attrs.ground_contact: ADWR verbatim: 'the State will not approve new determinations of Assured Water Supply within the Phoenix AMA based on groundwater supplies. Developments within existing Certificates or Designations of Assured Water Supply may continue' and 4.86 maf projected unmet demand over 100 years; 2024 update: 'Unmet demand has gone up in the Designation of Assured Water supply, Industrial, and Agricultural sectors.' The subdivider scoping is my reading of A.R.S. § 45-576, read directly — the two-hop conclusion is INFERRED and labelled as such.

nodes.label: No federal effluent floor exists for data centres — all discharge limits are site-specific
nodes.source_location: 40 CFR 423.10(a) applicability; corroborated by empty EffluentGuidelines object at https://echodata.epa.gov/echo/dfr_rest_services.get_dfr?p_id=110072132708&output=JSON

attrs.missing_or_defect: The steam-electric effluent guidelines do not apply — Part 423 covers establishments 'whose generation of electricity is the predominant source of revenue', and a data centre CONSUMES electricity. Consequence: 100% of a direct discharger's limits are water-quality-based effluent limits derived from the receiving stream, and 100% of an indirect discharger's numeric limits are POTW local limits. There is no technology-based floor to look up.
attrs.remedy: Model the receiving stream and obtain the sewer-use ordinance during diligence. Never benchmark chemistry against Part 423 — real permits run 10-60x tighter on total residual chlorine.
attrs.ground_contact: OPEN regulation, read directly via eCFR API. verbatim 423.10(a): 'The provisions of this part apply to discharges resulting from the operation of a generating unit by an establishment whose generation of electricity is the predominant source of revenue or principal reason for operation'. TRC comparison from real permits: Amazon VA0093301 0.016 mg/L daily max; Google GA0038920 0.01; Microsoft GA0050346 0.05; versus 40 CFR 423.13(d) 0.5 mg/L max free available chlorine. CAVEAT: ELG limits free available chlorine, permits limit total residual chlorine — directionally sound, not strictly like-for-like.

nodes.label: Discharge permit conditions can oppose cooling optimisation and cap buildable IT capacity
nodes.source_location: Amazon Data Services Northeast Creek VA0093301 limits effective 2026-02-01 to 2031-01-31; Microsoft GA0050346 limits 2025-05-01 to 2030-04-30

attrs.missing_or_defect: Two mechanisms nobody teaches. (1) A permit can impose a MINIMUM hardness (>=150 mg/L as CaCO3) as an enabling condition, because aquatic-life criteria for Zn/Cd/Cu are hardness-dependent — this directly opposes the cooling-side instinct to soften makeup water to raise cycles of concentration. (2) A phosphorus MASS LOAD (8.34 lb/day daily avg, the signature of a TMDL wasteload allocation) cannot be diluted away: it caps blowdown volume and therefore caps IT load, unless inhibitor chemistry changes. Phosphonate scale inhibitors are standard tower chemistry.
attrs.remedy: Run the cooling water treatment design and the discharge permit strategy as ONE coupled optimisation, not as sequential handoffs between disciplines.
attrs.ground_contact: Primary permit data via EPA ECHO REST services, retrieved 2026-08-13. Amazon VA0093301 Outfall 001: temperature <=32 C daily max; DO >=4 mg/L; pH 6-9; hardness total as CaCO3 >=150 mg/L MINIMUM; zinc <=165 ug/L; cadmium <=1.4 ug/L; copper <=18 ug/L; TRC <=0.008 mo avg / 0.016 daily max; chloride and DOC monitor-only. Receiving water flagged EsaAquaticSpeciesFlg = Yes. Microsoft GA0050346: phosphorus total <=8.34 lb/d daily avg, <=12.51 lb/d daily max.

nodes.label: Whether cooling tower blowdown triggers Significant Industrial User status is textually unresolved
nodes.source_location: 40 CFR 403.3(v)(1)(ii) SIU definition; 40 CFR 401.11(n) noncontact cooling water definition

attrs.missing_or_defect: The 25,000 gpd SIU flow trigger expressly excludes noncontact cooling water, and tower blowdown is noncontact cooling water by definition. A textual reading says a data centre discharging hundreds of thousands of gpd of pure blowdown never crosses the flow threshold. But the 5% hydraulic capacity prong, Control Authority designation, and the § 403.5 prohibitions remain independently live. No resolving EPA guidance found.
attrs.remedy: Raise with the Control Authority early — SIU status determines whether an individual industrial user permit, self-monitoring and semiannual reporting apply, i.e. months of schedule turn on this.
attrs.ground_contact: AMBIGUOUS by construction. SIU verbatim: 'discharges an average of 25,000 gallons per day or more of process wastewater to the POTW (excluding sanitary, noncontact cooling and boiler blowdown wastewater)'. 401.11(n) verbatim (including the codified typo): 'The term noncontract cooling water means water used for cooling which does not come into direct contact with any raw material, intermediate product, waste product or finished product.' Note 403.5(b)(4) is written as a FLOW RATE prohibition, giving a POTW a basis to cap purely on hydraulic loading.

nodes.label: WRI Aqueduct is a screening tool with a stale vintage, not a current-conditions tool
nodes.source_location: Kuzma et al., Aqueduct 4.0, WRI Technical Note, August 2023 (files.wri.org 404s; read from a mirror)

attrs.missing_or_defect: Aqueduct's baseline water stress layer targets 2019 (source range 1979-2019); its groundwater table decline layer reflects 1990-2014 and 'has not been rerun since its original release in 2019'. For a 2026 siting decision in a basin under recent rapid growth it will not show the last decade of change — yet it is routinely cited as current.
attrs.remedy: Screen with Aqueduct, then pair with state agency data before relying on it. Thresholds: baseline water stress >80% extremely high, 40-80% high, 20-40% medium-high; groundwater table decline >8 cm/yr extremely high.
attrs.ground_contact: definition verbatim: 'Baseline water stress measures the ratio of total water demand to available renewable surface and groundwater supplies.' Vintage metadata read directly from the technical note.

nodes.label: Water objections convert the cooling design rather than blocking the project
nodes.source_location: Tucson Project Blue sequence 2025-08-06 to 2026-08-05; Chile Cerrillos ruling; Uruguay Canelones

attrs.missing_or_defect: Water risk is modelled as a binary block. In every documented case the project was redesigned to air cooling and proceeded. The real question is not 'will water block us' but 'will water force a closed-loop redesign, and what does that cost in capex, PUE, and therefore MW'.
attrs.remedy: Price the air-cooled redesign as the expected outcome of water opposition, and carry its PUE/MW consequence back into the interconnection request.
attrs.ground_contact: Tucson: council voted unanimously 2025-08-06 to end negotiations; Ordinance 12188 adopted 2025-08-20 requiring users above 7.4 million gallons/month to apply and demonstrate conservation; developer kept the same 290 acres in unincorporated Pima County; ADWR approved wells totalling 96.50 acre-feet/year on 2026-05-28 with the facility redesigned to closed-loop air cooling; Tucson adopted data-centre regulations 6-1 on 2026-08-05, stopping short of a moratorium. Chile Second Environmental Court ordered the assessment reverted 'to incorporate consideration of the effects of climate change in the assessment of the water component' and suggested 'a possible modification of the cooling system of the servers'; Google had already filed an air-cooled redesign.

nodes.label: Water figures require a provenance tag — the disagreements live in metric definition
nodes.source_location: 2025-12-10 Chandler AZ reporting; corroborating cases The Dalles OR, Missoula County MT, Fayetteville GA

attrs.missing_or_defect: Measurement integrity is the weak link across this entire domain. Chandler lists five buildings as 'unknown'; Missoula County's moratorium cited 'contradictory water use figures' as a stated cause; Fayetteville GA found two unaccounted-for connections (~30 million gallons unbilled); The Dalles has an unresolved 355 vs 274.5 Mgal gap for the same year. The Project Blue 1,910 vs 96.5 AF/yr 'discrepancy' is not a source conflict at all — it is two project configurations.
attrs.remedy: Tag every water number as self-reported / utility-billed / permit-licensed / modelled, and version by project configuration. Never reconcile two figures before checking whether they measure the same thing.
attrs.ground_contact: Chandler applicant verbatim: 'the numbers contained in the Sustainable Water Service Application were per the City's direction and do not represent the actual anticipated usage of the building.' and 'It's impossible to provide an accurate projection of water use, because they don't know what's going to be happening in them.' The Dalles: 355 Mgal / 29% of city consumption in 2021 rising to about 40% by 2026.

nodes.label: EPA ECHO NPDES permit and effluent limit REST services

attrs.remedy: Pull comparable facilities' actual permit limits before assuming what your limits will be — this is the only way to see real WQBELs given there is no ELG. Query trap: a CWA query on NAICS 518210 returns ~40 facilities but the large majority are CONSTRUCTION STORMWATER general permits (TXR15..., KSR12..., FLR2..., KYR1...), not process-water permits; only about 9 are individual process-water permits. Counting all 40 overstates by ~4x.
attrs.ground_contact: used first-hand to retrieve Amazon VA0093301, Google GA0038920, Microsoft GA0050346 and Walmart AR0050652 permit limits, 2026-08-13

nodes.label: 44 CFR 9.4 — 'critical action' expressly includes data storage centers

attrs.ground_contact: OPEN regulation, read directly. verbatim: 'Critical action means any action for which even a slight chance of flooding is too great. Critical actions include, but are not limited to, those which create or extend the useful life of structures or facilities: ... (3) Such as emergency operation centers, or data storage centers which contain records or services that may become lost or inoperative during flood and storm events; and (4) Such as generating plants, and other principal points of utility lines.'

nodes.label: The data-centre flood design basis is the 0.2% annual chance event, not the 1%
nodes.source_location: FEMA Policy: Federal Flood Risk Management Standard, September 2024, read directly

attrs.missing_or_defect: Site screening uses the Special Flood Hazard Area (1% annual chance) as the pass/fail line. Federal regulation classifies data centres as critical actions, and FFRMS holds critical actions to the 0.2% annual chance floodplain, or base flood elevation + 3 feet under the Freeboard Value Approach.
attrs.remedy: Adopt the 0.2% event as the design basis and say why. SCOPE CAVEAT: FFRMS binds federally funded actions; a privately financed campus is not legally bound. Its force is evidentiary — but it is what an insurer, lender or hyperscale tenant will reach for.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim: 'for critical actions the FFRMS floodplain will be at least as restrictive as the 0.2% AC flood elevation and corresponding horizontal floodplain' and 'Freeboard Value Approach (FVA): ... adding 2 feet to the base flood elevation (BFE) for non-critical actions (+2' FVA) and from adding 3 feet to the BFE for critical actions (+3' FVA).' Hierarchy: CISA first where available and actionable, otherwise FVA / 0.2PFA.

nodes.label: Levee-protected land is accredited to the wrong flood event
nodes.source_location: 44 CFR 65.10, mapping of areas protected by levee systems

attrs.missing_or_defect: An accredited levee is certified to the base flood (1%) plus three feet of freeboard, and FEMA explicitly disclaims any statement about actual performance. A data centre's own federal tier is the 0.2% event — so the levee is accredited to the wrong event. Land behind an accredited levee maps as reduced-risk and is therefore cheap; that discount IS the residual risk being transferred to the buyer.
attrs.remedy: Treat 'levee-protected' as an elevated diligence trigger requiring independent hydraulic analysis, never as a mitigant.
attrs.ground_contact: OPEN regulation, read directly. verbatim: 'The FEMA review will be for the sole purpose of establishing appropriate risk zone determinations for NFIP maps and shall not constitute a determination by FEMA as to how a structure or system will perform in a flood event.' and 'Riverine levees must provide a minimum freeboard of three feet above the water-surface level of the base flood.'

nodes.label: FEMA maps understate flood risk — two quantifications that must not be averaged
nodes.source_location: Wing et al., Environmental Research Letters 13(3), 2018-02-28; and First Street Foundation via https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/first-street-foundation-releases-new-data-disclosing-the-flood-risk-of-every-home-in-the-contiguous-us-301084757.html (2020-06-29)

attrs.missing_or_defect: Wing 2018 reports a 3.2x ratio on PEOPLE in the 1% floodplain (41M vs 13M). First Street reports a 1.7x ratio on PROPERTIES at substantial risk (14.6M vs 8.7M). Different denominators, models and vintages — averaging them produces a meaningless number. They agree on mechanism: unmapped areas, pluvial flooding not depicted on FIRMs, and the stationarity assumption.
attrs.remedy: Treat 'Zone X, not in the SFHA' as a screening result, never a clearance. Commission site-specific hydrologic/hydraulic analysis plus an on-site stormwater study regardless of FIRM zone.
attrs.ground_contact: Wing verbatim: 'the total US population exposed to serious flooding is 2.6-3.1 times higher than previous estimates, and that nearly 41 million Americans live within the 1% annual exceedance probability floodplain (compared to only 13 million when calculated using FEMA flood maps).' First Street verbatim: 'While FEMA classifies 8.7 million properties as having substantial risk... the First Street Foundation Flood Model identifies nearly 70% more, or 14.6 million properties with the same level of risk.'

nodes.label: Soft soil invalidates the simplified seismic code path and forces a site-specific study
nodes.source_location: USGS seismic design web service, queried first-hand 2026-08-14 for Memphis TN (35.1495, -90.0490), ASCE 7-16, Risk Category III

attrs.missing_or_defect: Soft soil is modelled as 'costs more'. In fact at a real US location Site Class E returns NO design coefficients at all and Site Class D returns a partial answer, both pointing to a site-specific ground motion procedure. That specialist study lands on the critical path and cannot begin until the geotech knows Vs30 — which is the real reason geotech is a long-lead item, not the drilling calendar.
attrs.remedy: Scope the geotech to deliver Vs30 explicitly and early. Treat Site Class D/E as a schedule event, not a cost line.
attrs.ground_contact: FIRST-HAND MEASUREMENT, reproducible. Site Class A: SDC D, S_DS 0.546, S_D1 0.185. B: D, 0.614, 0.185. C: D, 0.819, 0.347. D: SDC null, S_DS 0.744, S_D1 null, fv_note 'See Section 11.4.8'. E: all null, fa_note and fv_note 'See Section 11.4.8'. Service erp-design-ws v1.2.2. NOTE: 'Section 11.4.8' is quoted as the API's own returned string; ASCE 7-16 was NOT read and no claim is made about that section's contents. Separately, USGS's national measured Vs30 compilation covers only 2,997 US sites — national Vs30 maps are overwhelmingly modelled from proxies.

nodes.label: Data-centre seismic/wind Risk Category assignment is contested (II vs III/IV)

attrs.missing_or_defect: The pro-III/IV position is a published PE argument, not a code requirement (note the author's own hedge, 'should really govern'). The counter-position is that codes assign III/IV on public life-safety grounds, so a private commercial data centre defaults to II. UNGROUNDED on the code side — IBC Table 1604.5 and ASCE 7 Table 1.5-1 are paywalled and were NOT read; no table content is quoted anywhere.
attrs.remedy: Force the decision into the open at concept design with the AHJ and insurer. It is far cheaper to design for III/IV than to retrofit to it.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim pro-position: 'if a data center is to be designed to Uptime's Tier III or IV standard, then Risk Category IV (Immediate Occupancy / Operational) should really govern the structural design.' PRECISE AXIS OF DISAGREEMENT: does 'essential facility' status derive from public life-safety function (the codes' basis) or from mission-criticality to the owner (the operator's basis)?

nodes.label: Risk Category is a cascading cost fork that switches an entire tornado chapter on or off
nodes.source_location: ICC describing ASCE 7-22 Chapter 32; wind return periods via https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5988364/

attrs.missing_or_defect: Risk Category is taught as a seismic importance factor. It also moves the wind design event from a 700-year to a 3,000-year mean recurrence interval (RC II to RC IV), determines whether ASCE 7-22's mandatory tornado provisions apply AT ALL (they apply to RC III and IV in the tornado-prone region), and cascades into nonstructural anchorage scope where the cost usually lands.
attrs.remedy: Teach Risk Category as a single decision with three cascading consequences, settled at concept design. Note ASCE 7-22 design tornado speeds correspond only to roughly EF0-EF2 — it is not protection against a violent tornado, and ICC 500 storm-shelter scope does not list data centres.
attrs.ground_contact: SECONDARY throughout — ICC and peer-reviewed literature DESCRIBING ASCE 7; ASCE 7 itself was not read. verbatim (ICC): 'Chapter 32 is a dedicated, mandatory tornado-load procedure for Risk Category III and IV structures inside the tornado-prone region.' verbatim (peer-reviewed): 'wind maps in ASCE 7-16, which are based on return periods of 300, 700, 1,700, and 3,000 years for Risk Categories I, II, III, and IV, respectively'.

nodes.label: Data-centre floor load design basis is contested — 100 to 435 psf across sources

attrs.missing_or_defect: Four sources answer three different questions: ASCE 7-22's 100 psf is a LEGAL MINIMUM for generic 'computer use — access floor systems'; UFC 3-301-01 gives 150 psf as government facility criteria; Intel recommends 350 psf as vendor high-density guidance; and a single modern AI rack lands at roughly 412-435 psf on its own footprint. Designing to the code minimum is designing to fail.
attrs.remedy: Design to the actual rack roadmap, not to the occupancy code minimum. Verify rack weights against OEM datasheets.
attrs.ground_contact: STRUCTURE article read directly — worked example verbatim: total '77,340 pounds spread out in a 16-x20-foot area. This is equivalent to approximately 240 psf, about 60% higher than the minimum specified by ASCE.' ASCE/UFC/Intel values are the article's transcription; those standards were NOT read. GB200 NVL72 at 3,000 lb in 600mm x 1,068mm is a DCIM vendor blog figure (medium confidence), and the ~435 psf is my arithmetic on it. EXPLICITLY REJECTED: a widely repeated '150 lbf/ft2 minimum / 250 lbf/ft2 recommended' attribution to TIA-942 — the citing page 404'd and TIA-942 is paywalled and unread; do not attribute those numbers to a TIA clause.

nodes.label: PSPS is a planned multi-day de-energisation invisible to utility reliability indices
nodes.source_location: CPUC on the October 2019 PG&E event; compliance findings at https://www.cpuc.ca.gov/news-and-updates/all-news/cpuc-holds-pge-accountable-for-flawed-implementation-of-fall-2019-psps-events

attrs.missing_or_defect: PSPS is a deliberate, planned, multi-day de-energisation, so it is excluded from SAIDI/SAIFI as a major-event day. A site can hold an excellent published reliability record and still face scheduled multi-day outages — during exactly the fire-weather conditions that also stress cooling. And advance warning is not dependable: CPUC found utilities failed to notify approximately 50,000 customers across three events.
attrs.remedy: Size generator fuel storage and resupply for PSPS duration, not storm-outage duration. Check PSPS programme status — it is no longer California-only; Washington and Oregon programmes are live.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim: 'PG&E's decision to shut off power during the week of October 7, 2019, affected more than 700,000 customers and impacted an estimated 2 million people.' Compliance verbatim: utilities 'failed to comply with CPUC-required guidelines in many of their 2019 PSPS events... the failure of PG&E's website, which was unavailable or non-functional during the majority of the duration of a PSPS event, the inaccuracy of PG&E's online outage maps... and PG&E's failure to provide advanced notification of PSPS events to approximately 50,000 customers'. Washington verbatim: 'Public Safety Power Shutoff Programs are new to Washington.'

nodes.label: Wildfire exposure is partly financial, through the power supplier's balance sheet
nodes.source_location: California FAIR Plan high-value commercial limits; inverse condemnation and AB 1054 via secondary sources

attrs.missing_or_defect: Two commercial exposures nobody teaches alongside the physical hazard. (1) California's FAIR Plan high-value commercial option caps at $20M per building and $100M per location and sunsets in 2028 — far below a hyperscale campus's insured value, so the residual market is not a backstop for this asset class, and the non-renewal moratorium is residential-only. (2) Under inverse condemnation, California utilities face strict liability for fire damage from their equipment regardless of negligence, with the majors contributing $10.5bn to the AB 1054 fund — so a long-term PPA counterparty in these territories carries catastrophic third-party liability exposure.
attrs.remedy: Include insurance capacity and PPA counterparty creditworthiness in wildfire diligence, not just defensible space and hazard maps.
attrs.ground_contact: FAIR Plan verbatim: 'New "high-value" commercial coverage became available July 26, 2025, covering properties with limits up to $20 million per building and $100 million maximum per location. This temporary option sunsets in 2028.' Inverse condemnation and AB 1054 figures are SECONDARY (search summaries, direct fetch blocked) — medium confidence.

nodes.label: The 180-day All Appropriate Inquiries list has five items, not three

attrs.missing_or_defect: A widely circulated summary lists only interviews, lien searches and government records on the 180-day clock. The regulation lists five — it also includes VISUAL INSPECTIONS of the facility and adjoining properties, and THE ENVIRONMENTAL PROFESSIONAL'S DECLARATION. Those two are the expensive, calendar-consuming components, so a stale Phase I needs substantive re-work, not a cheap paper update. POST-CLOSING: on an already-closed site the AAI clock has run and cannot be retroactively cured, and the bona fide prospective purchaser defence depends on having done it correctly BEFORE acquisition.
attrs.remedy: Propagate the five-item list. Audit the closed transaction's Phase I timing now, not at the next transaction.
attrs.ground_contact: OPEN regulation, read directly. verbatim: components to be conducted or updated 'within 180 days of and prior to the date of acquisition' are '(1) Interviews with past and present owners, operators, and occupants; (2) Searches for recorded environmental cleanup liens; (3) Reviews of federal, tribal, state, and local government records; (4) Visual inspections of the facility and of adjoining properties; and (5) The declaration by the environmental professional'. Outer window: AAI 'must be conducted within one year prior to the date of acquisition'.

nodes.label: Retired generation brownfields are interconnection assets, not just liabilities
nodes.source_location: US DOE, 2025-01-14; MISO retirement figure at https://www.energy.gov/oe/clean-energy-resources-meet-data-center-electricity-demand

attrs.missing_or_defect: Contamination is treated as a reason to avoid a site. In a market where the binding constraint is interconnection queue time rather than land, a retired coal plant offers an existing high-voltage point of interconnection, an existing switchyard, heavy-haul road and rail access, industrial zoning, and often water rights. The BFPP defence is specifically designed to make the contamination survivable.
attrs.remedy: When the answer to 'we cannot find a site with power' is a greenfield further out, the better answer is usually a contaminated site with a switchyard. Screen EPA's RE-Powering Mapper ('pre-screened over 190,000 sites').
attrs.ground_contact: DOE verbatim: 'Many retired and retiring coal power plants have attributes that are valuable for reinvestment, such as access to multiple forms of transportation and a point of interconnection to the electricity grid... Reinvestment options include wind plus storage, solar plus storage, nuclear power, data centers, and energy-related industrial uses.' Scale verbatim: 'Since 2010, MISO has experienced the retirement of 30.8 gigawatts (GW) of generation capacity, a large proportion of which (21.9 GW) was coal-fired generating units.' BFPP verbatim (EPA): 'A BFPP may purchase property with knowledge of contamination and still be eligible for liability protection... could purchase a contaminated property on CERCLA's National Priorities List or undergoing active cleanup and still maintain the liability protection'.

nodes.label: Vapour intrusion must be resolved before the slab is poured or it becomes permanent
nodes.source_location: EPA 2015 vapor intrusion technical guide (referenced); inference is mine

attrs.missing_or_defect: A large data hall is a big, mechanically ventilated, slab-on-grade structure. Sub-slab depressurisation retrofits under an energised data hall are effectively impossible, so an unresolved vapour intrusion pathway becomes permanent at slab pour. This sequencing consequence is not stated in any source found.
attrs.remedy: Sequence vapour intrusion resolution ahead of slab pour explicitly in the CPM schedule, alongside entrance-room geometry and MMR siting which have the same 'permanent after the envelope closes' property.
attrs.ground_contact: INFERRED engineering consequence, labelled as such. EPA guidance and ASTM E2600 (paywalled, scope page only) identify the pathway; neither states the retrofit-impossibility consequence for data halls.

nodes.label: 14 CFR 77.9 — FAA notice surfaces for construction or alteration

attrs.missing_or_defect: Routinely missed. At about two miles from a major runway the notice threshold is roughly 200 ft above runway elevation and drops linearly on approach. Generator exhaust stacks, cooling towers, comms masts and — most commonly missed — CONSTRUCTION CRANES all trip it. The shielding exemption requires being 'in the congested area of a city, town, or settlement', which a greenfield campus generally is not.
attrs.remedy: Run the 100:1 / 50:1 / 25:1 arithmetic at concept design and include temporary construction equipment.
attrs.ground_contact: OPEN regulation, read directly. verbatim: notice required for '(a) Any construction or alteration that is more than 200 ft. AGL at its site.' and surfaces of '100 to 1 for a horizontal distance of 20,000 ft. from the nearest point of the nearest runway' (longest runway over 3,200 ft), '50 to 1 for a horizontal distance of 10,000 ft.' (3,200 ft or less), '25 to 1 for a horizontal distance of 5,000 ft.' (heliports).

nodes.label: PUE measurement level relocates the same losses between numerator and denominator

attrs.missing_or_defect: PDU and distribution losses sit in the IT denominator at Level 1 and in the overhead numerator at Level 3. Same building, same electricity, different published PUE, and no rule compels disclosure of which level was used.
attrs.remedy: Never accept a PUE without its level/category. Write the required level into the design brief and the metering scope of work.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim Table 1: IT equipment energy is measured at UPS outputs (Level 1), PDU outputs (Level 2) or IT equipment input (Level 3); total facility energy is utility inputs at every level; intervals are monthly/weekly, daily/hourly, and continuous (<=15 minutes). Verbatim: 'To report Level 1, Level 2, or Level 3, the required measurement location for that level must be used.'

nodes.label: A PUE without its subscript is 'Unrecognized' under The Green Grid's own scheme

attrs.missing_or_defect: Essentially every published PUE is a bare scalar, i.e. Unrecognized by the metric's author.
attrs.remedy: Demand the subscript. Its absence is itself the finding.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim: PUE is reported as PUE_{a,b} where a is the metering placement level and b is the averaging period plus collection frequency (e.g. '2.1 PUE L3,YC'). Verbatim: 'The Unrecognized classification consists of reported results where the reporting organization has not provided any additional detail as to how and for how long the data was collected or the granularity with which the result's individual data points were collected.'

nodes.label: Design PUE is not a measurement — The Green Grid says so in terms

attrs.missing_or_defect: Design PUE quoted as achieved PUE is the single most common deception in the domain and the primary source explicitly disowns it.
attrs.remedy: Ask 'measurement or estimate, and over which dates'. Put a demonstrated-PUE acceptance test with a named averaging window into the EPC contract, not a design target.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim: 'Many published PUE numbers are not measurements, but rather estimates made by engineers for hypothetical conditions, such as for data centers under construction or for IT loads other than the actual IT loads. These projections, while useful, are not considered measurements or results under The Green Grid guidelines.' Also verbatim: 'Many PUE claims seem too good to be true and cause others to wonder if they are incorrectly obtaining their PUE values.'

nodes.label: Power-sampled PUE and energy-integrated PUE are different numbers

attrs.missing_or_defect: An instantaneous kW-based PUE taken on a cold night is a legitimate-looking number that means nothing about the year.
attrs.remedy: Require energy (kWh) integration and an annual averaging period; reject spot readings.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim: 'a daily sample of power will only provide PUE at the time of the sample, but a daily sample of energy will provide an accumulated or averaged PUE over the entire day. These two methods provide different results for a data center where the day-night outdoor temperature or IT equipment use varies significantly and for a data center that employs economizer cooling modes.' TGG's reporting guidelines define PUE as an energy metric, and constrain the allowed combinations (monthly collection only supports a yearly averaging period).

nodes.label: PUE varies with outdoor temperature and with IT load, so the reporting window IS the claim

attrs.missing_or_defect: Winter-only and low-load-only quoting are both invisible in a bare annualised-looking scalar.
attrs.remedy: Ask for the twelve months covered and the IT load as a percentage of installed capacity, then ask specifically for the hottest quarter.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim: 'A data center's location can have a significant impact on its PUE. The efficiency of identical mechanical systems can be drastically different depending on the climate in which the system operates.' and 'A typical data center's PUE is likely to vary with the levels of its IT load.' Figure 6 plots PUE against outdoor temperature at constant IT load.

nodes.label: pPUE is always lower than facility PUE by construction

attrs.missing_or_defect: A cooling-zone pPUE of 1.06 quoted as a facility PUE is arithmetically guaranteed to flatter.
attrs.remedy: Ask 'whole facility or a zone'. If a zone, ask for N0.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim derivation: PUE = N0/(I1+I2) + r1*pPUE1 + r2*pPUE2, where N0 is shared overhead outside any zone and ri is the zone's share of total IT energy. A zone pPUE therefore excludes N0.

nodes.label: Shared-plant apportionment is where a mixed-use PUE is actually decided

attrs.missing_or_defect: Without that metering, shared overhead can be assigned to the non-data-centre tenant and the data-centre PUE improves with no physical change.
attrs.remedy: Specify the shared-plant sub-metering in the base build, not as a later retrofit.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim: a shared chilled-water plant requires a flow meter in the supply or return pipe plus supply and return temperature sensors, and Q = VHC * flow rate * dT * time / energy conversion. Reg. (EU) 2024/1364 Annex II 1(b) solves the analogous floor-area problem by pro-rating on rated power demand.

nodes.label: The EU's mandatory reporting mandates the most flattering PUE boundary

attrs.missing_or_defect: Measuring IT at the UPS puts downstream distribution losses into the IT denominator, so the EU dataset is systematically lower than an IT-input figure — and the regulation nowhere says the two are non-comparable.
attrs.remedy: When benchmarking against EU aggregates, restate your own PUE at the UPS boundary or the comparison is invalid.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim: E_IT 'shall be measured in accordance with the category 1 methodology for the calculation of the PUE set out in the CEN/CENELEC EN 50600-4-2 standard or equivalent. Data centres shall measure the combined annual energy consumption at every uninterruptible power system (UPS) connected to data centre information technology equipment.' Category 2 (PDU) is offered only as a fallback for facilities without a UPS.

nodes.label: The agreed cross-facility comparison basis is PUE Level 2, yearly, continuous

attrs.remedy: Specify PUE_{L2,YC} as the contractual definition. Anything else quoted as comparable is an assertion, not a measurement.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim Table 4: unit of measure Energy; frequency of measurement Continuous; averaging period Annual; data centre location of measurement 'Utility(ies) hand-off'; IT location of measurement 'PDU output'.

nodes.label: Google quantifies the boundary effect at a third of its own overhead

attrs.missing_or_defect: 1.09 versus 1.06 is a third of the entire overhead moved by boundary choice alone, on the same buildings in the same year. It is also disclosed voluntarily by one operator and by nobody else.
attrs.remedy: Use this as the worked example when teaching that PUE is a boundary statement before it is an efficiency statement. Note the exclusions too: ramping sites and sub-5 MW sites are outside the number.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim: 'In 2025, the average annual power usage effectiveness for our global fleet of data centers was 1.09.' 'PUE overhead energy in our PUE calculations includes energy used in substations, transformers, water treatment plants, accessory buildings (such as employee cafeterias and gyms) and office space.' 'We could strip all this out and have a PUE of 1.06 or less, but we believe it's better to measure--and optimize--all aspects of data center operations.' Also verbatim: the fleet figure is reported 'across all our large-scale data centers (once they reach stable operations)', campus figures need 'at least twelve months of data', and a '5 MW threshold for reporting' applies.

nodes.label: Headline PUE trends are sample composition, not efficiency
nodes.source_location: Uptime Institute Journal, 4 December 2023; corroborated by LBNL 2024 p.47

attrs.missing_or_defect: Two headline series move in opposite directions over the same period and both are explained by which facilities are in the sample. Neither measures whether any data centre got more efficient.
attrs.remedy: Never quote a fleet or national average PUE as evidence of efficiency change without the sample composition. Ask what entered and left the denominator.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim Uptime: annual averages 2.5 (2007), 1.98 (2011), 1.65 (2014), 'stuck in the 1.55 to 1.59 band' 2020-2023, and 'The biggest component in the flatlining of the headline PUE number is a richer geographical mix of surveyed data centers' — North America and Europe fell from two-thirds of respondents in 2018 to under half by 2023, hotter regions reporting above 1.7. Verbatim LBNL: US average PUE falls 1.6 (2014) to 1.4 (2023) and 'This decline is primarily due to the shift towards larger data centers (hyperscale, colocation) that have a lower PUE.'

nodes.label: Two official source-energy weighting factor sets give one facility two PUEs

attrs.missing_or_defect: A facility buying district cooling has two defensible PUEs depending on which taskforce's factor set is applied, and no disclosure requirement attaches to the choice.
attrs.remedy: If any non-electric energy enters the boundary, state the weighting factor set alongside the PUE.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim Table 5 (Global Task Force): electricity 1.0, natural gas 0.35, fuel oil 0.35, other fuels 0.35, district chilled water 0.4, district hot water 0.4, district steam 0.4. Verbatim Table 6 (US Regional Task Force): electricity 1.0, natural gas 0.31, fuel oil 0.30, other fuels 0.30, district chilled water 0.31, district hot water 0.40.

nodes.label: Every PUE boundary starts below the transmission and distribution losses
nodes.source_location: eGRID frequent questions; cross-read against WP#49 Table 1 (total facility energy = utility inputs)

attrs.missing_or_defect: 4.2% of the generation caused by a US facility is outside every PUE ever published, by design.
attrs.remedy: When comparing a data centre to a self-generating or behind-the-meter alternative, add grid losses back or the comparison is rigged toward the grid-supplied option.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim eGRID: 'The 2023 U.S. grid gross loss is 4.2% of electricity transmitted and distributed annually.' Verbatim WP#49: total facility energy is measured at utility inputs at every level.

nodes.label: PUE awards no credit for reuse or on-site generation, which is exactly why ERE exists

attrs.missing_or_defect: A site that reuses heat looks WORSE on PUE. Any incentive scheme keyed on PUE alone penalises heat reuse.
attrs.remedy: Never set a PUE target without a paired ERF/ERE target, or you have written an anti-heat-reuse clause by accident.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim WP#49: 'Unlike other measures, PUE awards no credits or percentage points for generating energy, recovering waste heat, etc. ... The minimum PUE is 1.0, the maximum is infinity.' Verbatim WP#29: 'One such specific area is data center waste energy reuse in a facility, with a resultant claimed PUE of less than 1.0. ... No reuse energy term is allowed in the calculation and, by definition, the lowest possible PUE is 1.0.'

nodes.label: ERE = (1-ERF) x PUE — multiplicative, not 'PUE minus reuse' — and ERE = 1.0 is ambiguous

attrs.missing_or_defect: ERF is normalised by TOTAL energy while PUE and ERE are normalised by IT energy, so subtracting ERF from PUE is simply wrong arithmetic — and a single ERE number cannot be read alone.
attrs.remedy: Always publish PUE and ERE together. Teach the multiplication, not a subtraction.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim: 'ERF = Reuse Energy / Total Energy'; 'ERE = (1-ERF) x PUE'; 'as ERF goes to 0 (no energy reuse), ERE will equal PUE'. Ranges verbatim: '1.0 <= PUE <= inf, 0 <= ERE <= inf, 0 <= ERF <= 1.0'. Worked example: IT 20,000 kWh, cooling 10,000, power loss 4,500, lighting 500, total 35,000, reuse 6,000 gives PUE 1.75, ERF 0.17, ERE 1.45. Verbatim: an ERE of 1.0 'could represent a very efficient design (PUE = 1.2) with a small amount of energy reuse (ERF = 0.17 ...) or an inefficient base design (PUE = 2.0) with a lot or energy reuse (ERF = 0.50)'.

nodes.label: Reuse only counts outside the control volume, and the test is 'does it lower PUE'

attrs.remedy: Apply the same test to any reuse claim: if it already showed up in PUE, it may not show up again in ERE.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim: 'Only when there is energy being reused outside the data center CV will it be considered for ERE as reuse energy. Any energy reuse inside the control volume is already being accounted for in a lower PUE. Using it to also calculate a lower ERE is essentially double counting'. And the test: 'if the technology causes a lower PUE, then it should not be considered as part of ERE.'

nodes.label: CUE = CEF x PUE, covers only Scope 1 and 2, and is explicitly source-based

attrs.missing_or_defect: CUE excludes embodied/lifecycle carbon by explicit design decision: 'attempting to determine the carbon generated in the manufacturing of the IT equipment and its subsequent shipping to the data center would make the metric far too difficult to measure, calculate, or use.'
attrs.remedy: Never let CUE stand in for the carbon footprint of a build. It is an operating-phase electricity metric.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim: 'CUE = Total CO2 emissions caused by the Total Data Center Energy / IT Equipment Energy'; 'CUE = CEF x PUE'; units 'kilograms of carbon dioxide (kgCO2eq) per kilowatt-hour (kWh)'; 'For now, CUE is specifically limited to Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions.'; 'regardless of the existence of on-site generation, CUE is a source-based (versus site-based) metric ... A site-based CUE would have little, if any, value.' Ideal value 0.0, no upper bound.

nodes.label: WUE has a site form and a source form, and only the site form is ever published
nodes.source_location: section III, equations 1-4 and Appendix A

attrs.remedy: Ask 'site or source' before reading any WUE number, and ask what EWIF was used.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim: 'WUE = Annual Water Usage / IT Equipment Energy'; units 'liters/kilowatt-hour (L/kWh)'. Verbatim: WUE is 'a site-based metric ... (similar to carbon Scope 1)' and WUE_source 'includes water used on-site and water used off-site in the production of the energy used on-site ... (similar to carbon Scope 2)'. Verbatim eq. 4: 'WUE_source = [EWIF x PUE] + Annual Site Water Usage / IT Equipment Energy'. Numerator includes humidification, cooling tower evaporation, blowdown and drift, and water used in energy production.

nodes.label: Indirect water is roughly ten times site water and no regime requires reporting it
nodes.source_location: 2024 US Data Center Energy Usage Report, pp.44-48 and pp.56-57

attrs.missing_or_defect: An operator publishing 'WUE 0.2 L/kWh' is publishing roughly four percent of the water its operation causes to be consumed, and is complying fully with every disclosure regime in force.
attrs.remedy: Compute WUE_source = EWIF x PUE + site WUE for the actual balancing authority before underwriting any water claim. LBNL's recipe (EIA-930 + EIA-923 + EIA water + EPA emissions) is reproducible.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim: 'In 2023, energy consumption by a data center translates to national average of 4.52 L/kWh of indirect water consumption, along with 0.34 kg/kWh emissions. In comparison, the average water intensity factor for electricity use in the U.S. overall is 4.35 L/kWh, while the emission factor is 0.35 kg/kWh of CO2 equivalent.' Against a modelled national SITE WUE that 'stays just over 0.36 L/kWh through 2023', rising to 'between 0.45 and 0.48 L/kWh' after 2023.

nodes.label: The same structural shift lowers national PUE and raises national WUE
nodes.source_location: 2024 US Data Center Energy Usage Report, pp.45-48, Figures 4.6 and 4.7

attrs.missing_or_defect: This is the clearest metric conflict in the domain and it is visible inside a single source's own figures: optimising the published PUE is, at the margin, a decision to consume more water.
attrs.remedy: Set PUE and WUE targets jointly with an explicit exchange rate, or the design team will silently optimise whichever one is in the scorecard.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim: 'The above discussion does not imply low site WUEs are necessarily good. In many cases, there are tradeoffs between low PUEs and low site WUEs. For example, water-cooled chillers and other evaporation-based cooling systems are generally more energy efficient than an air-cooled chiller or other waterless systems. While air-cooled chillers use no water, they use more energy.' In the same model run the migration to hyperscale/colocation drives average PUE from 1.6 (2014) to 1.4 (2023) while average WUE rises from just over 0.36 L/kWh to 0.45-0.48 L/kWh.

nodes.label: WUE cannot distinguish potable from reclaimed water even though the EU collects both
nodes.source_location: Annex II points 1(h) and 1(i); Annex III point (b)

attrs.missing_or_defect: A site on 100% reclaimed municipal effluent and a site on 100% potable drinking water post the same WUE. The potable split is collected and then discarded by the indicator.
attrs.remedy: Report W_IN-POT/E_IT alongside WUE. It is already being collected; publishing it costs nothing and is the number a community actually cares about.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim: W_IN is 'all water volumes that enter the data centre boundary'; W_IN-POT is 'all potable water sources that enter the data centre boundary'. Annex III then defines the published indicator as 'WUE = W_IN/E_IT'.

nodes.label: WUE is scarcity-blind, and the metric's own author has conceded it

attrs.missing_or_defect: A litre consumed in a stressed basin scores identically to a litre in a wet one under WUE, and no reporting regime pairs WUE with a stress indicator.
attrs.remedy: Pair every WUE figure with a basin water-stress score. Watch WUI, but do not cite its formula until it has been read.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim: TGG 'released a new Water Usage Impact (WUI) metric' as increased energy demand affects water resources; announced on thegreengrid.org 2025-10-29. The WUI document itself is login-gated and was not read.

nodes.label: Scope 2 requires dual reporting, and the two numbers can diverge completely

attrs.missing_or_defect: A single headline 'carbon neutral' figure is almost always the market-based number reported alone, which the standard forbids.
attrs.remedy: Always ask for both. If only one is offered, it is the flattering one.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim: 'Companies with any operations in markets providing product or supplier-specific data in the form of contractual instruments shall report scope 2 emissions in two ways and label each result according to the method: one based on the location-based method, and one based on the market-based method. This is also termed dual reporting.' Verbatim: 'A location-based method reflects the average emissions intensity of grids on which energy consumption occurs ... A market-based method reflects emissions from electricity that companies have purposefully chosen (or their lack of choice).'

nodes.label: The Scope 2 Quality Criteria decline to specify a matching interval, by design
nodes.source_location: Table 7.1 criteria 4 and 5; section 7.5 commentary on criteria 4 and 5

attrs.missing_or_defect: The standard's own text endorses a certificate market wider than the electricity market and delegates temporal granularity to whatever the certificate market already does — annual. The 24/7-versus-annual argument starts here, in the drafted design, not in a loophole.
attrs.remedy: Teach criteria 4 and 5 verbatim before any discussion of 24/7 CFE. Everything else is marketing.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim criterion 4: 'Be issued and redeemed as close as possible to the period of energy consumption to which the instrument is applied.' Verbatim section 7.5: 'This timing should be consistent with existing standards for the market where the contractual instruments exist.' Verbatim criterion 5: 'Be sourced from the same market in which the reporting entity's electricity-consuming operations are located'. Verbatim section 7.5: 'markets for unbundled certificates have often been less constrained than those for electricity itself. This larger market boundary for certificate use promotes broader areas of consumer choice and the building of renewable energy resources in the most economically viable locations.'

nodes.label: The EU Renewable Energy Factor can be driven to 1.0 with unbundled certificates
nodes.source_location: Annex II points 1(o)-(r); Annex III point (d)

attrs.missing_or_defect: There is no temporal matching requirement and no deliverability requirement. A site on a coal-heavy grid every hour of the year can report REF 1.0 by retiring enough unbundled GOs, and the published EU aggregate will show it as fully renewable. REF measures procurement, not consumption, and the delegated act does not say so.
attrs.remedy: Treat REF as a procurement disclosure. If you want a consumption claim, compute hourly matched CFE separately and publish the method.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim: 'E_RES-TOT is the sum of E_RES-GOO, E_RES-PPA and E_RES-OS'; E_RES-GOO is 'the sum of the Guarantees of Origin purchased and retired by the reporting data centre'; 'REF = E_RES-TOT/E_DC'. The integrity conditions in the text are entirely about double counting — no instrument counted by two data centres, GOs created from a PPA must be owned and retired by the reporter or subtracted.

nodes.label: German law mandates 100% renewable 'bilanziell' — annual matching, in one word

attrs.missing_or_defect: 'Bilanziell' means on a balance-sheet basis, i.e. annual accounting matching, not hourly delivery. The hardest data-centre statute in force still picks annual matching.
attrs.remedy: Do not read a national 100%-renewable mandate as an hourly CFE mandate. Read the adverb.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim: 'Betreiber von Rechenzentren decken den Stromverbrauch in ihren Rechenzentren bilanziell 1. ab dem 1. Januar 2024 zu 50 Prozent durch Strom aus erneuerbaren Energien und 2. ab dem 1. Januar 2027 zu 100 Prozent durch Strom aus erneuerbaren Energien.'

nodes.label: Neither eGRID rate family answers the question a new large load asks

attrs.missing_or_defect: A new 300 MW interconnecting load is neither existing electricity use nor a displacement project. Using an average subregion factor for a campus siting decision is a category error dressed as diligence, and eGRID does not claim otherwise.
attrs.remedy: Use eGRID subregion rates for the location-based Scope 2 disclosure. For the marginal question, use a long-run marginal dataset and say which one.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim: subregion output rates are for 'estimating emissions from electricity use'; non-baseload output rates, 'sometimes called marginal emission rates because these rates are representative for plants on the margin of operation', are to 'estimate the emissions that could be avoided through projects that displace marginal fossil fuel generation, such as energy efficiency efforts and/or renewable energy'. 26 subregions that 'replicate the physical constraints of the electricity grid'.

nodes.label: The EU Directive names carbon usage effectiveness; the delegated act drops it
nodes.source_location: recital 192 of Directive (EU) 2023/1791, read against Annex III of Reg. (EU) 2024/1364

attrs.missing_or_defect: The carbon dimension named in the Directive's own recital did not survive into the implementing measure. CUE is standardised (ISO/IEC 30134-8:2022) and mandated by nobody.
attrs.remedy: Do not assume EU reporting produces a carbon number. It does not. Carbon disclosure for these operators comes from CSRD/ESRS and national regimes, not from the data-centre scheme.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim recital 192: the collected data should measure 'how efficiently it uses energy, how much of that energy comes from renewable energy sources, the reuse of any waste heat that it produces, the effectiveness of cooling, the effectiveness of carbon usage and the usage of freshwater.' Annex III of the delegated act defines exactly four indicators: PUE, WUE, ERF, REF. There is no carbon indicator, no emission factor and no Scope 2 requirement anywhere in the delegated act.

nodes.label: Annual matching said 100% while hourly matching said 61% — and 3% at one site
nodes.source_location: Google, '24/7 by 2030: Realizing a Carbon-free Future', September 2020, pp.6 and Appendix

attrs.missing_or_defect: The same portfolio is 100% renewable under annual matching and 61% carbon-free under hourly matching, with a 93-point spread across sites (3% to 96%). Annual matching added 22 points over the untouched grid mix (39% to 61%); the remaining 39 points of the '100%' claim are accounting.
attrs.remedy: This is the disagreement, quantified by the party that benefits from the looser convention. Ask any 100%-renewable claim for its hourly CFE score and its worst site.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim: 'Although we matched 100% of our global, annual electricity consumption with renewable energy in 2019, on an hourly basis 61% of all the electricity we used was matched with regional, carbon-free sources. Without Google's purchases of renewable energy this figure would have only been 39%, equivalent to the existing grid mix in regions where we operate.' And: 'In Singapore, most grid electricity comes from natural gas, and our data center was only matched with 3% carbon-free energy. In breezy Oklahoma ... our purchases of wind power helped drive carbon-free energy performance at our data center to 96%.'

nodes.label: Even the hourly CFE score is upward-biased, and its author says so

attrs.missing_or_defect: The regional grid CFE percentage counts carbon-free generation that other parties have already contracted, because no residual-mix dataset exists at global scale. So the 61% is itself generous, by an unquantified amount.
attrs.remedy: When a CFE percentage is quoted, ask whether the grid term uses residual mix or gross mix. If residual-mix data does not exist for that region, the number is an upper bound.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim: 'Google typically defines regional grid mix as encompassing all generating resources under a given balancing authority, including resources that might be under contract by specific parties via PPAs. While we recognize this can lead to double-counting issues, there is currently no consistent data available to help us evaluate residual mix across our global portfolio.' Also verbatim endnote 4: 'In calculating a data center's hourly match with regional carbon-free energy (CFE), we first count Google's renewable Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs).'

nodes.label: Once you buy renewables, embodied carbon becomes 82% of the data-centre footprint
nodes.source_location: Gupta et al., 'Chasing Carbon: The Elusive Environmental Footprint of Computing', HPCA 2021, Figure 2 and contribution 3

attrs.missing_or_defect: PUE, WUE, CUE, ERF and REF all measure the operating phase. On the operator's own published accounting that phase is 18% of the footprint — and CUE's authors excluded lifecycle carbon explicitly because it was 'far too difficult to measure'.
attrs.remedy: Require a building and hardware LCA alongside the operating metrics. A campus proposal that optimises PUE and ignores embodied carbon is optimising the minority term.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim from Figure 2: Facebook's 2018 data-centre carbon footprint is opex 65% / capex 35% WITHOUT renewables and capex 82% / opex 18% WITH renewables. Verbatim contribution 3: 'In 2019, for instance, capex- and supply-chain-related activities accounted for 23x more carbon emissions than opex-related activities at Facebook.' The paper defines capex-related emissions as 'emissions from facility-infrastructure construction and chip manufacturing (e.g., raw-material procurement, fabrication, packaging, and assembly)'.

nodes.label: The embodied share is partly an artefact of market-based Scope 2 accounting
nodes.source_location: Gupta et al., HPCA 2021, Figure 2 (the same figure gives both splits)

attrs.missing_or_defect: 'Embodied carbon is now 82% of our footprint' is simultaneously true and a consequence of choosing market-based Scope 2. Under location-based accounting the same facility reads 35%.
attrs.remedy: State which Scope 2 method the embodied share was computed against. An embodied-share percentage without that qualifier is not interpretable.
attrs.ground_contact: The same source gives capex 35% without renewables and capex 82% with renewables for the same facility in the same year. The physical embodied emissions did not change; the denominator did, because purchased renewables drive the reported operational term toward zero.

nodes.label: The figure '1.8 L/kWh' names two completely different quantities
nodes.source_location: NREL/TP-550-33905 (Torcellini, Long & Judkoff, December 2003) p.1, read against LBNL-1005775 (2016) p.~35

attrs.missing_or_defect: The same number is a SOURCE water intensity of electricity in one document and a SITE water intensity of a data centre in the other. Anyone reconciling two '1.8 L/kWh' figures without checking which is which will silently combine incompatible quantities.
attrs.remedy: Never write '1.8 L/kWh' without the words 'site' or 'source' attached. Treat any unqualified 1.8 in a data-centre water calculation as a defect until the boundary is established.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim NREL 2003: 'In thermoelectric plants, 0.47 gal (1.8 L) of fresh water is evaporated per kWh of electricity consumed at the point of end use.' verbatim LBNL 2016: 'on-site water consumption is estimated at 1.8 liters (0.46 gallons) per kWh of total data center site energy use'. Both extracted byte-for-byte from the source PDFs.

nodes.label: The Green Grid's default EWIF excludes hydropower twice over
nodes.source_location: NREL/TP-550-33905, December 2003, p.1, read against TGG WP#35 Appendix A

attrs.missing_or_defect: TGG adopted the THERMOELECTRIC-ONLY figure as a national average and then also set hydro to zero — excluding hydro reservoir evaporation twice. NREL's own combined national figure in the same sentence is 7.6 L/kWh, over 4x the TGG default. This is the mechanism behind the 1.8-versus-4.35 disagreement.
attrs.remedy: If you use an EWIF, state whether hydro reservoir evaporation is in or out, and do not use TGG's 1.8 default as a national average — it never was one.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim NREL 2003: thermoelectric 0.47 gal (1.8 L)/kWh; 'Hydroelectric plants evaporate an average of 18 gal (68 L) of fresh water per kWh used by the consumer. The national weighted average for thermoelectric and hydroelectric water use is 2.0 gal (7.6 L) of evaporated water per kWh of electricity consumed at the point of end use.' TGG WP#35 takes 1.8 L/kWh as its US 'unknown' default AND separately assigns Hydro an EWIF of 0.

nodes.label: Scarcity-weighting more than doubles the water footprint — and the method already exists
nodes.source_location: Siddik, Shehabi & Marston, Environmental Research Letters 16(6), 1 June 2021, section 3.2

attrs.missing_or_defect: A peer-reviewed, published scarcity-weighted water footprint for US data centres has existed since 2021 and gives a number more than double the volumetric one — and no reporting regime, metric or curriculum uses it. The industry is not waiting on a method; it is declining to use one that exists.
attrs.remedy: Compute and publish a scarcity-weighted water figure alongside WUE. The 17.9-vs-7.1 gap is the number a permitting authority will eventually ask for.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim: 'Nationally, we estimate that 1 MWh of energy consumption by a data center requires 7.1 m3 of water. However, this national average masks the large spatial variation (range 1.8-105.9 m3)'. verbatim: 'Roughly three-fourths of US data centers' operational water footprint is from indirect water dependencies.' verbatim: 'The WSF (including both direct and indirect water requirements) per unit of energy consumption is 17.9 m3 US-eq water MWh-1, more than double the nationally averaged water intensity (7.1 m3 MWh-1) that does not account for water scarcity. WSFs that are larger than volumetric water footprints suggest that data centers disproportionately utilize water resources from watersheds experiencing greater water scarcity than average.'

nodes.label: Water withdrawal and water consumption differ by about thirtyfold

attrs.missing_or_defect: A withdrawal figure and a consumption figure for the same facility differ by roughly 30x. Objectors quote withdrawal; operators quote consumption; both are correct and they are not comparable. WUE as defined measures neither explicitly.
attrs.remedy: State withdrawal AND consumption separately for every water number in a proposal, and expect the other side to use whichever is larger.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim: 'Withdrawals for thermoelectric power were 133 Bgal/d in 2015' and 'Total consumptive use for thermoelectric power was 4.31 Bgal/d in 2015 or 3 percent of the total thermoelectric-power withdrawals.'

nodes.label: Hourly procurement beats annual matching by 84-120% in California, 7-29% in PJM
nodes.source_location: Xu, Manocha, Patankar & Jenkins, 'System-level Impacts of 24/7 Carbon-free Electricity Procurement', ZERO Lab / Princeton, 16 November 2021, Key Findings

attrs.missing_or_defect: These figures are widely re-quoted as 'the Joule paper found'. They are not in the paper that was read. Cite the 2021 report for the numbers and the 2024 article for the peer-reviewed qualitative claim.
attrs.remedy: Use the region-specific spread, not a single headline: the advantage of hourly matching is about an order of magnitude larger in a high-VRE grid (California) than in PJM.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim: '100% CFE achieves 84%-120% greater emissions reductions than 100% annual matching' (California) and '100% CFE achieves 7%-29% greater emissions reductions than' 100% annual matching (PJM). Also verbatim: '100% annual matching reaches a CFE of 75% in California and 62% in PJM.' ATTRIBUTION WARNING: these percentages are from the 2021 ZERO Lab report, NOT from the peer-reviewed Joule 2024 article (Xu, Ricks, Manocha, Patankar & Jenkins, Joule 8(2):374-400, DOI 10.1016/j.joule.2023.12.007), whose body is paywalled and was NOT read. The Joule abstract states only the qualitative result.

nodes.label: Below a high CFE target, annual matching cuts emissions MORE deeply

attrs.missing_or_defect: The pro-24/7 result is CONDITIONAL on a very high CFE target. Below the 88%/92% crossover the volume effect dominates and annual matching wins on emissions. This caveat is almost never carried with the headline percentages, and it inverts the procurement recommendation for any buyer not chasing ~90%+ CFE.
attrs.remedy: Ask what CFE target a 24/7 recommendation assumes. Below the crossover, buying more MWh matters more than matching them hourly.
attrs.ground_contact: verbatim: 'For California (PJM) with 10% C&I participation rate, 24/7 procurement cuts emissions more deeply than 100% annual matching for CFE targets of 88% (92%) or greater.' The report attributes this to two competing effects, verbatim: '(1) a timing effect, in which CFE supply is better matched to demand ... and (2) a volume effect where a larger/smaller total quantity of CFE generated by the procured resources displaces more/less emitting generation'. It also concedes verbatim that 'alternative procurement strategies optimized to maximize generation during periods of high grid carbon intensity rather than match demand may deliver greater overall emissions reductions.'
