nodes.label: Uptime awards ONE site rating, governed by the weakest relevant subsystem
nodes.source_location: paragraph beginning 'A data center either meets all the criteria'

attrs.missing_or_defect: Verbatim: 'A data center either meets all the criteria for a specified Tier or it doesn't. For example, if you have a Concurrently Maintainable electrical infrastructure but only a single distribution path mechanical system, then advertising to your senior management that you are "Tier III" can only lead to ultimate disappointment.' A flawless electrical topology cannot buy a Tier the mechanical plant does not support.
attrs.remedy: Electrical topology decisions must be taken jointly with mechanical topology, or the electrical spend is stranded.
attrs.ground_contact: Full text extracted from the Uptime Professional Services PDF and read

nodes.label: EN 50600 assigns availability classes separately per subsystem, not one site class

attrs.missing_or_defect: Verbatim: 'Four different grades of availability classes are defined for EN 50600-2-2 (electrical system), EN 50600-2-3 (mechanical system), EN 50600-2-4 (cabling system).' A facility can legitimately be AC4 electrical and AC2 mechanical. Uptime's system has no grammar for that statement, so 'Class 4' heard as 'Tier IV' silently discards the mechanical and cabling qualifiers.
attrs.remedy: Any EN 50600 claim must be written as a triple {electrical AC, mechanical AC, cabling AC}. A bare 'Class 3' is an incomplete claim and should be rejected in procurement.
attrs.ground_contact: Full text extracted from the TUV NORD whitepaper and read

nodes.label: EN 50600 contains no evaluation scheme, so its certificates are not comparable

attrs.missing_or_defect: Verbatim: 'Auditors and inspection teams are not included because the EN 50600 standard is designed as a guideline. Therefore, it does not include an evaluation scheme which is necessary for neutral, comparable and consistent assessments. A lack of an official defined evaluation scheme causes data center evaluators to come up with their own interpretation which results in assessments offered in the market to be different and not comparable.' Named problems: no clear requirements by degree of risk, no evaluation instructions or scope specification, and 'no coordination body for the auditors'. TUV NORD states 'assessments based solely on the EN 50600 standard without the criteria catalog are therefore not recommended.'
attrs.remedy: For any EN 50600 certificate, demand the certification body's criteria catalogue and its scope of testing. Two AC3 certificates from two CBs are not the same claim.
attrs.ground_contact: Full text extracted from the TUV NORD whitepaper and read

nodes.label: EN 50600 AC4 is 'fault tolerant except during maintenance'

attrs.missing_or_defect: TUV NORD renders AC4 as 'Multi path design / fault tolerant except during maintenance'. Uptime Tier IV requires that BOTH tests hold - no impact from a single worst-case failure AND every element removable on a planned basis - plus physical compartmentalization. AC4 and Tier IV therefore make materially different promises about the maintenance state.
attrs.remedy: If the business requires fault tolerance while a component is out for service, that is a 2(N+1)-shaped requirement and must be stated explicitly; no level label conveys it.
attrs.ground_contact: TUV NORD whitepaper read in full (secondary source; the EN 50600 clause text is PAYWALLED and was not read)

nodes.label: Tier IV requires complementary paths to be physically compartmentalized

attrs.missing_or_defect: Verbatim from this third-party rendition of Uptime's published tier material: 'Complementary systems and distribution paths must be physically separated (compartmentalized) to prevent any single event from impacting on both systems and paths simultaneously.' Compartmentalization is a room/containment property, not a component count - so it cannot be met by adding modules.
attrs.remedy: Model enclosures (rooms, duct banks, busway runs, containment) as explicit nodes; a 2N plant in one electrical room is not compartmentalized.
attrs.ground_contact: Full text extracted from a publicly posted third-party rendition of Uptime tier material (uploaded 2023-07). The Tier Standard itself is PAYWALLED and was NOT read; this is a SECONDARY source.

nodes.label: Uptime removed expected-downtime-per-year from the Tier Standard in 2009

attrs.missing_or_defect: Verbatim: 'In 2009, Uptime Institute removed all references to "expected downtime per year" when using the Tier Standard. The current Tier Standard of Topology does not assign availability predictions to Tier levels.' Retired figures nonetheless remain in active circulation.
attrs.remedy: Reject any tier-keyed uptime percentage in an SLA, contract or design basis; require a measured or modelled availability with its own assumptions.
attrs.ground_contact: Quoted extract returned from the Uptime journal explainer page

nodes.label: TIA replaced 'Tier' with 'Rated' in the 2014 revision at Uptime's request

attrs.missing_or_defect: Both systems originally used 'Tier' for four levels (Uptime Roman, TIA Arabic). In 2013 Uptime asked TIA to drop the term; the 2014 revision uses 'Rated/Rating'. Any post-2014 document saying 'TIA-942 Tier 3' is using retired nomenclature.
attrs.remedy: Use document date as a competence signal when reviewing vendor claims; 'TIA Tier 3' dates the author, not the facility.
attrs.ground_contact: Summarised extract from EPI's public history article

nodes.label: Tier Certification is three distinct awards at three lifecycle stages

attrs.missing_or_defect: Tier Certification of Design Documents (TCDD, stated as valid for two years), Tier Certification of Constructed Facility (TCCF, verified on site by test), Tier Certification of Operational Sustainability (TCOS, assesses operations and management). A TCDD is a drawing set, not a building; a self-declared 'Tier III design' is none of the three.
attrs.remedy: Procurement must capture stage, certificate ID and issue date. Treat 'Tier III' with no stage named as self-declared until proven otherwise.
attrs.ground_contact: Quoted extracts from the Uptime journal explainer page

nodes.label: Component count does not determine Tier level; distribution paths do

attrs.missing_or_defect: Verbatim: 'Increasing the component count does not determine or guarantee achievement of any specific Tier level, because Tiers also includes evaluation of distribution pathways and other system elements.' Uptime states a facility can achieve Tier IV with N+1 components if the distribution paths are right. Also: 'Tier Certification is a performance-based evaluation of a data center's specific infrastructure; it is not a checklist or cookbook.'
attrs.remedy: Stop specifying resilience as a redundancy ratio. Specify it as a set of pass/fail behaviours over failure and maintenance scenarios.
attrs.ground_contact: Quoted extracts from the Uptime journal myths page

nodes.label: Concurrent maintainability and fault tolerance are properties over different event classes
nodes.source_location: Tier III and Tier IV performance confirmation tests and operational impact

attrs.missing_or_defect: Concurrent maintainability is over PLANNED events: 'each and every capacity component and element of the distribution paths can be removed from service on a planned basis without causing any of the equipment to be shut down.' Fault tolerance is over UNPLANNED events: 'a single worst case failure of any capacity system, capacity component or distribution element will not impact the equipment.' Tier III's own stated operational impact is 'the site is susceptible to disruption from unplanned activities' and 'operation errors or spontaneous failures of site infrastructure components may cause a facility disruption.'
attrs.remedy: State the two requirements separately in the design basis. Buying Tier III is buying maintenance without downtime and ACCEPTING that an unplanned single failure can drop load.
attrs.ground_contact: Full text extracted from a publicly posted third-party rendition of Uptime tier material; corroborated by uptimeinstitute.com/tiers wording on Tier III vs Tier IV

nodes.label: Resilience class is a function of current operating state, not a static plaque
nodes.source_location: Tier III and Tier IV operational impact

attrs.missing_or_defect: Even at Tier IV: 'During maintenance activities, the risk of disruption may be elevated.' The moment a component is pulled, an N+1 group is N and a 2N pair is N. A single static class label cannot express this, which is precisely why 2(N+1) and N+2 exist.
attrs.remedy: Model and report class per operating state: normal, each maintenance state, each post-fault state. Make the maintenance-state class an explicit design requirement.
attrs.ground_contact: Full text extracted from a publicly posted third-party rendition of Uptime tier material; corroborated by Schneider WP75 on 2(N+1) retaining redundancy during concurrent maintenance

nodes.label: Tier IV fault tolerance explicitly excludes fire alarm, suppression and EPO
nodes.source_location: Tier IV operational impact; summary table row 'Single point of failure'

attrs.missing_or_defect: The tier summary table lists Tier IV single points of failure as 'None + fire and EPO', and the Tier IV operational impact states 'Operation of the fire alarm, fire suppression, or Emergency Power Off (EPO) may cause a data centre disruption.' Life-safety systems sit outside the fault-tolerance envelope and can command the whole load off by design.
attrs.remedy: Include EPO and fire-alarm circuits as Control nodes in the cut-set model; a model that omits them will report a fault tolerance the standard itself does not claim.
attrs.ground_contact: Full text extracted from a publicly posted third-party rendition of Uptime tier material (SECONDARY; Tier Standard is PAYWALLED and was NOT read)

nodes.label: Isolated redundant adds 23 failure modes without moving unreliability (MTechnology PRA)
nodes.source_location: Isolated redundant section, MTechnology PRA paragraph

attrs.missing_or_defect: Verbatim: 'the isolated redundant system does not materially affect the probability of failure (unreliability.) Both systems had an unreliability of 1.8% per year of operation. The isolated redundant model resulted in 30 failure modes (minimal cut sets) vs. 7 for the capacity system.' Also: 'adding complexity and additional components to the system invariably increases the number of potential failure modes', and the analysis ignored human error and aging, which would worsen the isolated case.
attrs.remedy: Report cut-set COUNT alongside probability; they can move in opposite directions. Reject redundancy that adds cut sets without moving the risk number.
attrs.ground_contact: Full text extracted from Schneider Electric/APC White Paper 75 Rev 4 and read

nodes.label: A static transfer switch structurally couples the A and B paths

attrs.missing_or_defect: Verbatim: 'A best practice for redundant dual path architectures is to isolate both paths so that they are independent of each other so that a failure on one side can not propagate to the other side. The use of static transfer switches in dual path architectures prevents the isolation of both redundant paths.' Uptime independently records a site where an 'STS-PDU fault affecting one-third of its IT equipment' made the whole facility unavailable, and states the large-STS approach 'does not meet Tier III or Tier IV criteria'. Rack-mount transfer switches 'do not exhibit the failure modes that propagate faults upstream to multiple UPS system as is the case with larger STS'.
attrs.remedy: Model an STS as a shared-failure vertex joining A and B, never as a redundancy-adding node. Push transfer switching to the rack where single-corded load is unavoidable.
attrs.ground_contact: Full text of Schneider WP75 Rev 4 read; corroborated by quoted extracts from the Uptime dual-corded power article

nodes.label: The paralleling bus, board and controls are N+1's residual single point of failure
nodes.source_location: Parallel redundant or N+1 section, advantages/disadvantages list

attrs.missing_or_defect: Verbatim: 'even though these systems provide protection of a single UPS module failure, there still remains a single point of failure in the paralleling bus'; 'If service is required in the parallel board or the parallel controls or down-stream equipment, the load will be exposed to un-protected power'; 'Still single points of failure upstream and downstream of the UPS system'; 'Single load bus per system, a single point of failure'. Modules 'must be of the same design, same manufacturer, same rating, same technology and configuration' - which is itself a design/hardware coupling mechanism.
attrs.remedy: In the model, the paralleling control is a Control node shared by every module in the group, and the module group is a design/hardware CCCG.
attrs.ground_contact: Full text extracted from Schneider WP75 Rev 4 and read

nodes.label: A multi-source synchroniser can simultaneously drop every UPS it synchronises

attrs.missing_or_defect: Verbatim: 'adding a synchronisation unit on the output of independent UPS systems allows for the possibility of a failure that can simultaneously drop all UPS systems.' A device added to make transfers safer converts independent systems into one common cause component group.
attrs.remedy: If a synchroniser is used, declare it as an interfaces-class CCCG spanning every UPS on it and compute the cut sets with it collapsed.
attrs.ground_contact: Full text extracted from Schneider WP75 Rev 4 and read

nodes.label: 1-10% of servers may be mis-corded, silently defeating the dual path

attrs.missing_or_defect: Uptime records anecdotal evidence that '1-10% of servers in a data center may be improperly corded, i.e., both cords are plugged into the A distribution'. The specification also requires 'full equipment functionality when operating from A and B power sources or from A alone or from B alone' with 'no loss of data, reduction in hardware functionality, performance, capacity, or cooling', and that 'the normal load on each power source will be shared within 10% of the average'. Unbalanced A/B means the survivor is asked to carry a load it was not sized for at the instant of failure.
attrs.remedy: Treat the as-built cord map as a first-class data-quality asset with continuous verification; enforce and monitor the +/-10% A/B balance rule. The as-built graph is not the as-designed graph.
attrs.ground_contact: Quoted extracts returned from the Uptime journal dual-corded power article

nodes.label: Fuel systems are where a 2N plant most often has a genuine N node
nodes.source_location: single points of failure and shared infrastructure sections

attrs.missing_or_defect: Named exposures: 'a single valve between two pumps or storage tanks when using an N+1 configuration, which cannot be maintained without shutdown of more than the redundant number of components'; 'A single panel or single ATS feeding all fuel pumps is a common example'; fuel control panels lacking redundancy. And the arithmetic trap: an operator claiming 48 hours from 'two 24-hour tanks' actually has '24 hours of Concurrently Maintainable fuel'.
attrs.remedy: Model fuel as a Consumable with its own topology (tanks, pumps, day tanks, returns, controls, and the electrical panel feeding the pumps). Compute concurrently-maintainable fuel hours, not nameplate hours.
attrs.ground_contact: Quoted extracts returned from the Uptime journal fuel system article

nodes.label: Standby generation fails in the transition, not at rest - three public postmortems agree
nodes.source_location: cross-event synthesis of AWS 2012, AWS 2013, Google 2026

attrs.missing_or_defect: AWS 2012: 'the generators started successfully, but each generator independently failed to provide stable voltage as they were brought into service'. AWS 2013: 'during that failover a breaker in front of one of the generators opened, rendering that generator unavailable' plus 'a second generator independently failed due to a mechanical issue'. Google 2026: 'the DRUPS back-up power system for side A failed to take over the facility load due to electrical component failures'. In two of three, the failed element was a breaker or a control, not the prime mover.
attrs.remedy: Model generation as {engine, alternator, starting system, breaker, control} with the breaker and control as separate nodes. Weight commissioning and load-bank testing on the TRANSFER, and treat standby-group failures as demand-correlated, not independent.
attrs.ground_contact: Verbatim quotes returned from the three public postmortem pages, all read

nodes.label: A utility transient reaches both feeds: two feeds are one feed against upstream disturbance

attrs.missing_or_defect: Verbatim: 'A 3ms voltage drop in the power feed from the utility provider and subsequent utility breaker protective action', and 'A regional data center hosting services in europe-west4-a experienced an upstream voltage transient affecting both utility power feeds A and B.' Dual utility feeds are redundant against feed LOSS; they are a single shared node against a disturbance on the common upstream network.
attrs.remedy: Model the utility as a disturbance Source shared by all feeds (environment-class CCCG), separate from the per-feed availability node. Design so that a simultaneous both-side transfer is a survivable, tested state.
attrs.ground_contact: Verbatim quotes returned from the Google Cloud Service Health incident report

nodes.label: A controller dropping offline defeats cooling redundancy that never failed

attrs.missing_or_defect: Verbatim: 'The chiller controller dropped offline during the voltage transient event, failing to signal the chilled water distribution pumps to restart and ultimately causing the chiller system A to shut down.' The chillers themselves did not fail. The control logic was the failed element, and it was disturbed by the same event that demanded the transfer.
attrs.remedy: Controllers, BMS sequences and ATS logic are first-class nodes with 'controls' edges that are hard dependencies for cut-set purposes even though no power flows along them. Ride-through the control plane, not just the load.
attrs.ground_contact: Verbatim quote returned from the Google Cloud Service Health incident report

nodes.label: Recovery procedures propagate faults across isolation boundaries that held under failure

attrs.missing_or_defect: In sa-east-1 2013, after the power event 'a network technician brought a network device up manually in the power-impacted Availability Zone and introduced a bad configuration', degrading connectivity for BOTH Availability Zones. The isolation boundary survived the power failure and was dissolved by the recovery action.
attrs.remedy: Treat recovery procedures as a procedures-class coupling mechanism in the CCCG overlay. Rehearse recovery, not just failure.
attrs.ground_contact: Verbatim quote returned from the AWS post-event summary

nodes.label: Power remains the leading cause of significant outages, concentrated in UPS, transfer switches and generators

attrs.missing_or_defect: Reported pattern: power is the leading cause of impactful outages, with failures involving UPS systems, transfer switches and generators dominant; a ~43% figure for power-related significant outages is attributed to the 2022 analysis. The failure mass sits on TRANSFER and CONVERSION elements, not steady-state distribution.
attrs.remedy: Spend on independence of control and transfer logic before spending on another module on the bus.
attrs.ground_contact: UNGROUNDED - only an aggregated web-search summary of Uptime press releases was seen; the Annual Outage Analysis reports themselves were NOT read and are gated.

nodes.label: Topology names are not standardised and must never be contracted for by name

The problems with these terms are that they can mean different things to different people, and can be interpreted in different ways.'

attrs.ground_contact: Full text extracted from Schneider WP75 Rev 4 and read

nodes.source_location: LBNL 'Queued Up: Status and Drivers of Generator Interconnection Backlogs', J. Seel, April 2025

nodes.label: Claim: Tier III and Tier IV require all hardware to have dual power inputs
nodes.source_location: Tier III and Tier IV performance confirmation tests

Corroborated by Schneider WP75: 'tier IV power architectures require that all loads are dual-corded, including electrical feeds to air conditioning equipment.'
attrs.remedy: Make the single-corded-load inventory a gating design input; the day one single-corded appliance arrives, the correct topology changes.
attrs.ground_contact: Read verbatim in the third-party Uptime rendition and independently in Schneider WP75 Rev 4 (both SECONDARY; the Tier Standard is PAYWALLED and was NOT read)

nodes.label: Claim: Uptime requires a minimum of 12 hours of on-site fuel storage for Tier III/IV

attrs.missing_or_defect: Uptime's public journal states a minimum of 12 hours of fuel storage at design load for Tier III and IV, with supply and return paths meeting the same Concurrently Maintainable or Fault Tolerant bar. NOTE: this is Uptime's own public journal describing its paid standard - the standard clause was NOT read and no clause number is asserted.
attrs.remedy: Compute concurrently-maintainable fuel hours, not nameplate; verify the pump panel and pump ATS are not a shared node.
attrs.ground_contact: Quoted extract from the Uptime journal fuel article (secondary description of a PAYWALLED standard)

nodes.label: Claim: N+1 tolerates one failure - true only under the independence antecedent

attrs.missing_or_defect: The claim carries an unstated antecedent: the failure is INDEPENDENT and the system is in its normal state. CCF theory names the two ingredients: 'A CCF is the result of the existence of two main factors - a failure cause and a coupling factor (or mechanism). ... The coupling factor (or coupling mechanism) creates the condition for a failure cause to affect multiple components thereby producing a CCF.' Coupling mechanisms per NUREG/CR-5485: 'design, hardware, function, installation, maintenance, procedures, interfaces, locations, and environment.'
attrs.remedy: State the antecedent every time. Public postmortems where redundancy 'failed' are almost always antecedent violations, not counterexamples to the redundancy pattern.
attrs.ground_contact: Verbatim text extracted from the open-access arXiv paper, which cites NUREG/CR-5485

nodes.label: Google Cloud europe-west4-a power and cooling outage, 2026-07-15

attrs.missing_or_defect: 'Incident began at 2026-07-15 16:57 and ended at 2026-07-16 05:25 (all times are US/Pacific).' Sequence: 3ms utility voltage drop plus utility breaker protective action; upstream transient affects BOTH feeds A and B; side B transfers to DRUPS cleanly; side A DRUPS 'failed to take over the facility load due to electrical component failures'; chiller controller drops offline and fails to restart chilled water pumps; chiller system A shuts down; ambient temperature rises and hosts/storage/network are shut down to prevent damage.
attrs.remedy: CORRECT CHARACTERISATION: common-mode initiating event + demand-correlated standby failure + control-plane dependency crossing the power/cooling boundary. This is NOT a counterexample to N+1 or 2N; it is a violation of the independence antecedent at three shared layers.
attrs.ground_contact: Verbatim quotes returned from the Google Cloud Service Health incident report

nodes.label: AWS sa-east-1 power event, 2013-12-17

attrs.missing_or_defect: 'the impacted Availability Zone lost utility power due to a fault that happened at the substation of the local utility provider'; 'the load switched over to our backup generators as designed'; 'during that failover a breaker in front of one of the generators opened, rendering that generator unavailable'; 'a second generator independently failed due to a mechanical issue'; then 'a network technician brought a network device up manually in the power-impacted Availability Zone and introduced a bad configuration' degrading connectivity across both AZs.
attrs.remedy: CORRECT CHARACTERISATION: multiple-failure sequence under a shared start command (function/demand coupling), followed by human-mediated cross-domain propagation through the recovery action. Not an N+1 counterexample.
attrs.ground_contact: Verbatim quotes returned from the AWS post-event summary page

nodes.label: AWS us-east-1 power event, 2012-06-29

attrs.missing_or_defect: 'At 7:24pm PDT, a large voltage spike was experienced by the electrical switching equipment in two of the US East-1 datacenters supporting a single Availability Zone.' One datacenter transferred cleanly; in the other 'the generators started successfully, but each generator independently failed to provide stable voltage as they were brought into service'. 'The utility power in the Region failed a second time at 7:57pm PDT. Again, all rooms of this one facility failed to successfully transfer to generator power.' UPS depleted; 'servers began losing power at 8:04pm PDT'.
attrs.remedy: CORRECT CHARACTERISATION: common-cause failure of a generator group (identical behaviour across the group under identical demand, repeated on a second event - the textbook CCCG signature) plus finite ride-through. UPS ride-through is a clock, not a redundancy.
attrs.ground_contact: Verbatim quotes returned from the AWS post-event summary page

nodes.label: Lesson: redundancy dies at the shared control layer, which the one-line does not draw
nodes.source_location: synthesis of Google 2026, AWS 2013, AWS 2012 and Schneider WP75

attrs.missing_or_defect: Chiller controllers, paralleling boards, source synchronisers, ATS logic, BMS sequences, fuel control panels and EPO circuits are shared by construction and invisible on a power one-line diagram. Every large public power postmortem in this fragment turns on one of them.
attrs.remedy: Draw a second diagram: the control dependency graph. Require it at design review with the same seriousness as the one-line.
attrs.ground_contact: Cross-source synthesis of four documents read in full or in quoted extract

nodes.label: Lesson: 'tolerates one failure' means one INDEPENDENT failure from the normal state

attrs.missing_or_defect: Analysts repeatedly mis-report common-mode events as evidence that redundancy 'does not work'. It is the wrong lesson and it drives the wrong spend (more modules) instead of the right spend (independence of controls, separation of enclosures, decorrelation of demand).
attrs.remedy: Every redundancy claim in the curriculum and in the model carries its antecedent explicitly. Every postmortem is classified as independent-failure, common-cause, or antecedent-violation before conclusions are drawn.
attrs.ground_contact: Grounded in the open-access CCF definitions and applied to three public postmortems read in this session

nodes.label: Capacity (N) UPS topology

attrs.missing_or_defect: Model nodes: utility -> ATS -> UPS -> maintenance bypass -> PDU -> load. Tolerates nothing: 'An N configuration system is essentially comprised of a series of single points of failure.' Maintenance exposes the load: 'usually takes place at least once a year with a typical duration of 2 - 4 hours'. Every element is a 1-element cut set.
attrs.remedy: Only defensible where geographic redundancy carries availability; WP75 notes 'two remote data centers with 1N redundancy are likely to be more available than a single highly redundant data center'.
attrs.ground_contact: Full text of Schneider WP75 Rev 4 read

nodes.label: Parallel redundant (N+1) UPS topology

attrs.missing_or_defect: Model nodes: identical modules on one paralleling bus, with a paralleling board/control node shared by all. Tolerates: loss of one module, provided survivors accept the transferred load instantly. Does NOT tolerate: paralleling bus, board or control failure; anything upstream or downstream; service on the parallel board. CCCGs: design/hardware (identical make, model, rating, firmware), function (shared control), location (shared room and battery room).
attrs.remedy: Declare the module group as a design/hardware CCCG and the paralleling control as a shared Control node before computing cut sets.
attrs.ground_contact: Full text of Schneider WP75 Rev 4 read

nodes.label: N+2 redundancy
nodes.source_location: derived from Tier III/IV maintenance-state discussion and WP75 N+x definition

attrs.missing_or_defect: Tolerates two concurrent module losses, which in practice means one failure WHILE one module is out for maintenance - the exact state N+1 does not cover. Does not change the shared bus or controls, so it buys maintenance-window safety, not path redundancy.
attrs.remedy: Choose N+2 when the requirement is 'survive a failure during planned maintenance' on a single bus; choose 2(N+1) when the requirement is that plus path independence.
attrs.ground_contact: INFERRED from the read Tier maintenance-state language plus WP75's N+x definition; no single source states this framing verbatim

nodes.label: Isolated redundant / catcher UPS topology

attrs.missing_or_defect: Model nodes: primary UPS carries load; catcher UPS feeds the primary's static bypass input. Tolerates a primary fault ONLY IF the primary's static bypass operates AND the catcher accepts an instantaneous step from 0% load. Named dependencies: 'Reliance on the proper operation of the primary module's static bypass'; 'both UPS modules' static bypass must operate properly to supply currents in excess of the inverter's capability'; 'Single load bus per system, a single point of failure'. 30 minimal cut sets vs 7 for plain capacity, at identical 1.8%/yr unreliability.
attrs.remedy: Avoid at scale. If inherited, model the static bypass path as a mandatory series element in every survival path and report the cut-set count explicitly.
attrs.ground_contact: Full text of Schneider WP75 Rev 4 read, including the MTechnology PRA result

nodes.label: Distributed redundant / tri-redundant / block-redundant topology

attrs.missing_or_defect: Model nodes: three or more UPS blocks with independent input and output feeders; loads reach blocks via multiple PDUs, optionally via STS; a 'catcher' variant leaves block 3 unloaded to catch either primary. Tolerates loss of one block for dual-corded load. Does NOT tolerate STS failure where STS are used, nor loss of a second block. Stated disadvantages: 'Design relies on the proper operation of the STS equipment which represents single points of failure and complex failure modes'; load-balance management difficulty; 'the system has many operating modes and many possible transitions between them. It is difficult to test all of these modes under anticipated and fault conditions.'
attrs.remedy: Model per operating state, not just normal. Declare STS and any synchroniser as A/B coupling vertices. Chosen for multi-MW sites where concurrent maintenance is required and UPS-count savings over 2N matter.
attrs.ground_contact: Full text of Schneider WP75 Rev 4 read

nodes.label: System plus system (2N, 2(N+1)) topology
nodes.source_location: System plus system redundant section, Figure 7

attrs.missing_or_defect: Model nodes: two complete paths from separate switchboards, ideally separate utility services and separate generator plants, to dual-corded load. Tolerates any single component failure on one side. In 2(N+1) specifically: 'UPS redundancy still exists, even during concurrent maintenance' - the property that distinguishes it from 2N and the one most often not asked for. Does not tolerate anything acting on both sides at once. Explicit limitation: 'typical buildings are not well suited for large highly available system plus system installations that require compartmentalizing of redundant components'.
attrs.remedy: Buy 2(N+1) when the maintenance-state class must remain redundant. Enforce compartmentalization physically; a 2N plant in one electrical room is not what the diagram claims.
attrs.ground_contact: Full text of Schneider WP75 Rev 4 read

nodes.label: Static transfer switch (STS)

attrs.missing_or_defect: Two inputs, one output, transfer 'in about 4 to 8 milliseconds'. Model as a Transfer node with attributes {transfer_time_ms, requires_source_sync, fail_state} that JOINS the A and B trees - it is a coupling vertex, not a redundancy node. Upstream-of-PDU placement is cheaper and less reliable than low-voltage placement downstream of two PDUs.
attrs.remedy: Prefer no STS with 100% dual-corded load. Where single-corded load exists, prefer many small rack-mount switches to one large STS.
attrs.ground_contact: Full text of Schneider WP75 Rev 4 read; corroborated by the Uptime dual-corded article

nodes.label: Rack-mount (point-of-use) transfer switch

attrs.missing_or_defect: Uptime states the Tier Standard permits 'a local, rack-mounted transfer switch' for legacy single-corded devices, distributing risk as low as possible in the distribution chain. Schneider adds that 'distributed rack-mount transfer switches do not exhibit the failure modes that propagate faults upstream to multiple UPS system as is the case with larger STS'.
attrs.remedy: Where single-corded load is unavoidable, push the transfer to the rack. Model each as a small local coupling vertex affecting only its own racks.
attrs.ground_contact: Quoted extract from the Uptime dual-corded article; corroborated by WP75 full text

nodes.label: Dual-corded A/B rack distribution
nodes.source_location: fault tolerance requirements at rack level

attrs.missing_or_defect: Requirements as published: full functionality on A+B, A alone or B alone with 'no loss of data, reduction in hardware functionality, performance, capacity, or cooling'; A/B load 'shared within 10% of the average'; and prohibition of 'internal or external active AC input switching devices (e.g., mechanical or electronic transfer switches)' inside the equipment. This is the terminal node of the whole electrical graph and the one least monitored.
attrs.remedy: Continuous cord-map verification and A/B balance monitoring; treat the as-built map as model input, not documentation.
attrs.ground_contact: Quoted extracts from the Uptime dual-corded article

nodes.label: Automatic transfer switch (ATS)

attrs.missing_or_defect: Model as a Transfer node with a DECISION (logic) sub-node and a MECHANISM sub-node - the two fail differently and independently. Uptime's fuel article names the archetypal misuse directly: 'A single panel or single ATS feeding all fuel pumps is a common example' of a fuel-system single point of failure.
attrs.remedy: Enumerate every ATS in the plant including non-IT ones (fuel pumps, controls panels, mechanical plant); those are the ones that silently span both sides.
attrs.ground_contact: WP75 full text read for topology placement; Uptime fuel article quoted for the shared-ATS failure mode

nodes.label: Diesel generator plant and fuel system
nodes.source_location: single points of failure, contamination, Tier requirements

attrs.missing_or_defect: Model as {engine, alternator, starting system, breaker, control} plus a fuel sub-graph {bulk tanks, pumps, valves, day tanks, return path, control panel, pump power source} plus a Consumable node with a depletion rate. Named exposures: single valve between two pumps or tanks; single panel or single ATS feeding all fuel pumps; non-redundant fuel control panels; contamination requiring treatment to 'remove water, algal growth and sediment'.
attrs.remedy: Compute concurrently-maintainable fuel hours, not nameplate hours; require permanently installed fuel treatment; test on the transfer, not at rest.
attrs.ground_contact: Quoted extracts from the Uptime fuel article; transfer-failure evidence from three public postmortems read

nodes.label: Diesel rotary UPS (DRUPS)
nodes.source_location: DRUPS side A / side B behaviour

attrs.missing_or_defect: Kinetic ride-through with an engine in the same machine, so conversion and generation are mechanically coupled and there is no separate battery room. Public evidence of its failure signature: side B 'was successful without any power interruption' while 'the DRUPS back-up power system for side A failed to take over the facility load due to electrical component failures' - i.e. the same transfer-failure signature as a diesel plant, in a single asset.
attrs.remedy: Do not credit DRUPS with removing the transfer risk; it relocates it. Model the DRUPS as a combined Source+Conversion node whose failure removes both ride-through and generation together.
attrs.ground_contact: Verbatim quotes from the Google incident report. General DRUPS mechanics beyond this incident are NOT sourced here.

nodes.label: Li-ion vs VRLA UPS energy storage

attrs.missing_or_defect: Three modelling-relevant differences: (a) Li-ion adds a BMS, so the battery acquires a CONTROL dependency and the BMS becomes a graph node; (b) shorter designed runtime tightens coupling to generator-start reliability, which the postmortems say is the fragile step; (c) NFPA 855 governs the installation, so fire strategy, spacing and room construction interact with the Tier IV physical-compartmentalization requirement. Specific NFPA thresholds circulating in secondary sources were NOT verified.
attrs.remedy: Treat battery chemistry as an architecture decision, not a procurement one: it changes the control graph, the ride-through clock, and the room.
attrs.ground_contact: UNGROUNDED for the NFPA 855 specifics (search summary only). The BMS-as-control-node and ride-through-clock points are INFERRED from sources read in this session.

nodes.label: Busway versus conduit-and-whip final distribution

attrs.missing_or_defect: For cut-set purposes a busway run is an ENCLOSURE-scoped common-cause group: one run, one set of joints, one potential arc event across every rack fed from it. Two busways in the same containment, on the same support steel, above the same racks, are not two independent paths against physical events. Conduit trades change friction for physical separation.
attrs.remedy: Model busway runs as 'contains' enclosures, not as edges. Require A and B runs to be separated in the same way rooms are.
attrs.ground_contact: UNGROUNDED - no busway-specific source was read in this session. This is engineering reasoning applied to the WP75 hardening principle ('the two UPS systems would not reside in the same room'), which WAS read.

nodes.label: PDU and remote power panel (RPP)

attrs.missing_or_defect: Transformation plus branch protection plus monitoring. The governing failure mode is breaker coordination: WP75 states 'Circuit breaker coordination becomes a critical component of these designs. Proper circuit breaker coordination can prevent short circuits from affecting large portions of the building.' Mis-coordination is how a small downstream fault clears an upstream board and removes a whole path.
attrs.remedy: Treat the coordination study as a resilience deliverable with the same weight as the one-line, and re-run it whenever load or source impedance changes.
attrs.ground_contact: Full text of Schneider WP75 Rev 4 read

nodes.label: Utility service and MV distribution
nodes.source_location: root cause; plus WP75 hardening paragraph

attrs.missing_or_defect: Model the utility as TWO things: a per-feed availability Source and a shared upstream DISTURBANCE source. The Google event shows a 3ms drop plus utility breaker protective action reaching both feeds. MV assets fail rarely with long repair times and are where '2N' most often collapses into one duct bank, one manhole, one switch room.
attrs.remedy: Declare an environment-class CCCG over all feeds sharing an upstream network, and a location-class CCCG over every shared civil route.
attrs.ground_contact: Verbatim quotes from the Google incident report; hardening principle from WP75 full text

nodes.label: CCCG overlay: coupling-mechanism tagging for the plant graph

attrs.missing_or_defect: Common cause groups are NOT derivable from the feeds-graph; they come from physical and organisational facts the one-line does not carry. Tag groups by the nine mechanisms - design, hardware, function, installation, maintenance, procedures, interfaces, locations, environment - each with a data-centre instance: same UPS model both sides; same breaker batch; one chiller control sequence; one duct bank; one crew and one week; one wrong MOP applied twice; one BMS/EPMS/synchroniser; one room or busway run; one utility transient.
attrs.remedy: Make the CCCG list a mandatory, separately-populated, reviewed artifact. Without it the model systematically OVERSTATES resilience.
attrs.ground_contact: Verbatim CCF/CCCG/coupling definitions extracted from the open-access arXiv paper citing NUREG/CR-5485

nodes.label: Minimal cut-set model of the plant (typed dependency graph for cdcp_plant)

attrs.missing_or_defect: Node kinds: Source, Transfer, Conversion, Distribution, Load (including mechanical plant as both load and dependency), Control, Consumable. Edge kinds: feeds, controls (a hard dependency despite carrying no power), contains (enclosure scoping), consumes (with rate). Required outputs: (1) minimal cut sets by cardinality, each tagged independent vs CCCG-collapse; (2) cut sets per operating state - normal, each maintenance state, each post-fault state; (3) cut-set COUNT alongside probability; (4) ride-through budget per source-loss scenario.
attrs.remedy: Implement in cdcp_plant. The MTechnology result (30 cut sets vs 7 at identical 1.8%/yr unreliability) is the acceptance fixture: a model that cannot reproduce count-and-probability divergence is not modelling complexity cost.
attrs.ground_contact: Structure derived from sources read in this session: WP75 (cut sets, operating modes), arXiv CCF paper (CCCG), Google incident (control edges), Uptime fuel article (consumables)

nodes.label: Gap: Tier / Rated / Availability Class taught as a comparison table, not as three different claims

attrs.missing_or_defect: Curricula hand out an equivalence chart. They do not teach that the three systems evaluate different subjects, in different styles, at different scopes, certified by different mechanisms - with EN 50600 having no official evaluation scheme at all and Uptime rating the whole site at its weakest subsystem while EN 50600 rates subsystems separately.
attrs.remedy: Teach the eight axes of disagreement and the six-part procurement question {document, body, stage, certificate id and date, one-line, scope and weakest subsystem}. Assess by making students find the axis two given claims disagree on.
attrs.ground_contact: Derived from primary/secondary sources read in this session and their explicit mutual disagreements

nodes.label: Gap: common-cause failure theory is mature, free, and absent from data-centre training

attrs.missing_or_defect: CCF, CCCG, coupling mechanisms, alpha/beta factor models are standard in nuclear PRA and openly published, yet data-centre practitioners re-derive the concept from each new postmortem. The absence is why common-mode events get mis-reported as 'redundancy failed'.
attrs.remedy: Teach the nine coupling mechanisms with a data-centre instance for each, and require students to classify every studied outage as independent, common-cause, or antecedent-violation.
attrs.ground_contact: Open-access CCF literature read in this session; absence inferred from the framing of mainstream DC resilience material encountered

nodes.label: Gap: control-plane dependencies are absent from the diagrams students are taught to read

attrs.missing_or_defect: One-line diagrams draw power, not control. Controllers, BMS sequences, synchronisers, ATS logic, fuel control panels and EPO circuits are where redundancy actually dies, and they appear on no drawing in the standard curriculum.
attrs.remedy: Require a control dependency diagram as a distinct deliverable at design review, and teach cut-set computation over 'controls' edges.
attrs.ground_contact: Google incident report read; corroborated by WP75 on paralleling controls and synchronisers

nodes.label: Gap: resilience class is taught as a static plaque, not as a function of operating state

attrs.missing_or_defect: Even Tier IV concedes 'during maintenance activities, the risk of disruption may be elevated'. An N+1 group is N the moment a module is pulled. Students are never asked 'what class is this facility in RIGHT NOW?'
attrs.remedy: Teach the maintenance-state class as a design requirement, and teach why 2(N+1) and N+2 exist as answers to it.
attrs.ground_contact: Third-party rendition of Uptime tier material read; corroborated by WP75 on 2(N+1) retaining redundancy during concurrent maintenance

nodes.label: Gap: operators cannot enumerate the 2-element cut sets of their own plant

attrs.missing_or_defect: Reliability engineering treats minimal cut sets as routine; data-centre operations treats them as exotic. The published isolated-redundant result (30 cut sets vs 7 at identical unreliability) shows why count and probability must both be reported - and neither is taught.
attrs.remedy: Make cut-set enumeration a hands-on exercise on the student's own one-line, with a required CCCG declaration step.
attrs.ground_contact: WP75 full text read

nodes.label: Gap: cord-level verification and A/B load balance treated as a commissioning checkbox

attrs.missing_or_defect: A published 1-10% mis-cording rate and a +/-10% A/B balance requirement mean the as-built graph differs from the as-designed graph, continuously. This is a data-quality problem with an outage attached, and it is taught, if at all, as a one-time check.
attrs.remedy: Teach continuous cord-map verification and A/B balance monitoring as an operational control, and make the cord map an input to the resilience model.
attrs.ground_contact: Quoted extracts from the Uptime dual-corded article

nodes.label: Gap: fuel, state of charge and thermal mass taught as states rather than clocks
nodes.source_location: shared infrastructure / 48 hours from two 24-hour tanks

attrs.missing_or_defect: '48 hours of fuel' from two 24-hour tanks is really 24 concurrently-maintainable hours. UPS ride-through is a depleting budget, not a redundancy - AWS 2012 ends with 'servers began losing power at 8:04pm PDT'. Consumables are taught as availability booleans.
attrs.remedy: Teach consumables as rate-limited resources with a computed time-to-load-loss per scenario, and teach the concurrently-maintainable-hours arithmetic explicitly.
attrs.ground_contact: Uptime fuel article quoted extracts; AWS 2012 postmortem read

nodes.label: Gap: certification stage, scope and expiry are not taught, so buyers cannot interrogate a claim

attrs.missing_or_defect: TCDD (design documents, stated two-year validity) vs TCCF (constructed facility) vs TCOS (operational sustainability) vs self-declared are four different evidentiary strengths under one phrase; TIA-942 Ready is separately annual. Nobody teaches the buyer's interrogation.
attrs.remedy: Teach the four-way taxonomy plus the cross-standard confusions, and drill the six-part procurement question until it is reflexive.
attrs.ground_contact: Quoted extracts from the Uptime journal explainer and the TIA certifications page

nodes.label: Gap: students are not taught to check whether a claim was withdrawn by its own author

attrs.missing_or_defect: The tier availability percentages were removed by Uptime in 2009 and were still being published in a document uploaded in July 2023. The same pattern applies to 'TIA-942 Tier 3' after the 2014 rename.
attrs.remedy: Teach source dating and author-withdrawal checking as an explicit competence, with these two cases as the worked examples.
attrs.ground_contact: Retired figures read verbatim in a 2023-uploaded document; withdrawal statement read on Uptime's own journal

nodes.label: Gap: rack-level distributed energy storage breaks the facility-UPS-centric mental model

attrs.missing_or_defect: Hyperscale designs push energy storage into the rack power shelf, converting one large shared cut-set vertex into thousands of small independent ones and changing where the ride-through clock lives. Curricula are built around a central facility UPS.
attrs.remedy: Teach both models and, more importantly, teach how the cut-set structure differs between them. Requires reading the OCP specifications first.
attrs.ground_contact: UNGROUNDED - the OCP specification page returned HTTP 403 in this session and was NOT read. This gap is asserted from general awareness and must be grounded before it is taught.

nodes.label: Gap: single-corded load inventory is a topology decision made by procurement accident

attrs.missing_or_defect: The design that is correct for 100% dual-corded load is wrong the day one single-corded appliance arrives, and the remedy chosen (one big STS vs many rack-mount switches) has a large cut-set consequence. WP75: 'Placing hundreds of single-corded devices on a single large STS is an elevated risk factor.'
attrs.remedy: Teach single-corded inventory as a standing design input with a stated remedy policy, and connect it to the Tier III/IV dual-input requirement.
attrs.ground_contact: WP75 full text read; corroborated by the Uptime dual-corded article

nodes.label: Gap: EPO and fire-alarm circuits are omitted from resilience models that claim fault tolerance
nodes.source_location: Tier IV operational impact and single-point-of-failure row

attrs.missing_or_defect: The tier material itself lists Tier IV single points of failure as 'None + fire and EPO'. Models that omit these nodes report a fault tolerance the standard does not claim.
attrs.remedy: Include life-safety command paths as Control nodes; teach that fault tolerance is scoped to the electrical/mechanical topology and stops at the life-safety boundary.
attrs.ground_contact: Read verbatim in the third-party rendition of Uptime tier material

nodes.label: Gap: spend and teaching weight module count over transfer and control independence

attrs.missing_or_defect: The outage mass sits on UPS, transfer switches and generators - the transfer and conversion elements - while both curricula and capex arguments centre on how many modules are on the bus.
attrs.remedy: Reframe the resilience budget around independence of transfer and control logic; teach the postmortem evidence before teaching redundancy ratios.
attrs.ground_contact: Grounded in three postmortems read in full; the aggregate outage statistic itself is UNGROUNDED (search summary only).

nodes.label: L4 Mechanical & thermal

attrs.missing_or_defect: Scope: cooling topologies, liquid cooling, containment, thermal ride-through / continuous cooling, and mechanical control dependencies. Explicitly NOT: density trends (L2), water rights and sourcing (L1), electrical topology (L3).
attrs.remedy: Cover the mechanism, not the vocabulary. Emit Gap nodes generously; thermal is where the target curriculum is thinnest in mechanism.

nodes.label: Greenfield campus: land closed, cooling topology and ride-through budget undecided

nodes.label: ASHRAE Guideline 0 The Commissioning Process

attrs.missing_or_defect: The parent process document that data-centre Level 1-5 commissioning nomenclature is commonly traced to. Without it, the level definitions used below have no single open authority.
attrs.remedy: Requires a human to read the publication and enter the values manually. Do not let any agent fill this gap from a third-party summary — the third-party restatement is still ASHRAE IP and is still prohibited.
